RECORD-00061.summary: The article critiques the Republican primary debates of 2012, highlighting the disparity between the questions asked by journalists and the issues that voters are actually concerned about. It discusses a study by NYU's Studio 20 analyzing the topics covered in the debates and contrasts them with a "citizens agenda" approach, which prioritizes the concerns of the electorate. The author proposes shifting campaign coverage to better reflect the priorities of the public and encourages readers to suggest topics they want the candidates to discuss.
RECORD-00061.quote: We're interested in what we have previously called a "citizens agenda" approach to campaign coverage in 2012.
concepts: The Citizens Agenda
RECORD-00061.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00646.summary: Before the 1980s, the Republican Party was similar to the Democratic Party. The Great Realignment saw Ronald Reagan build a new coalition consisting of socially conservative Christians, the wealthy, and the Southern working class, united by exploiting social tensions. The Republican Party then shifted its focus from economic to social issues, fostering resentment towards groups considered the "liberal elite." After Reagan, the party found a new unifying force in attacking the government, though this created internal tension regarding popular programs. The Republican Party is now in crisis, divided by its inability to shrink the government while still protecting popular programs. The party's future is uncertain, possibly fracturing or fading away without a new way to unite its factions.
RECORD-00646.quote: The party is going to have to decide whether its future lies with the evangelical Christians of the heartland or with the secular, pro-business voters of the suburbs. It cannot be the party of both Rick Santorum and Mitt Romney. It has to choose.
concepts: Verification in reverse
Mindcasting
RECORD-00646.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00060.summary: The article discusses an effort by Guardian US and NYU's Studio 20 program to create a "citizens agenda" for the 2012 election coverage. This approach aims to shift the focus from the strategic game of who's going to win to what voters want the candidates to be discussing. It describes a project involving the public and local news organizations to identify key issues and hold candidates accountable to those priorities. The ultimate goal is to make campaign coverage more relevant and useful to the public.
RECORD-00060.quote: democracy is about participating, so let's extend that principle to the campaign news system and see if we can make it work.
concepts: The Citizens Agenda
RECORD-00060.author: Jay Rosen', 'Amanda Michel

RECORD-00649.summary: Journalism is undergoing a significant transformation due to technological advancements, evolving economic models, shifting audience expectations, and open-source culture. These changes present both challenges and opportunities. Serious journalism, upholding principles like transparency, accuracy, and accountability, is crucial, especially in the digital age. This involves curating information, fostering community engagement, and providing tools for civic action. Journalists must collaborate, innovate, and adapt, embracing new technologies and storytelling formats. A strong ethical foundation is essential to navigate the complexities of information in the digital landscape. Journalism students are entering a dynamic field and have the opportunity to shape the future of journalism by embracing new approaches, technologies, and community engagement strategies.
RECORD-00649.quote: Their comparative advantage is no longer in telling us what is happening, because we can learn this from multiple other sources. Rather, their real value-added will be in investigating and explaining why something is happening.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience
Audience atomization overcome
RECORD-00649.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00632.summary: Jay Rosen, author of "What Are Journalists For?", discusses investigative journalism's role after the 9/11 attacks in an interview with The World's Marco Werman.
RECORD-00632.quote: Why are some of the biggest names in journalism today also some of its greatest critics?
concepts: View from Nowhere
The Production of Innocence
RECORD-00632.author: Marco Werman

RECORD-00609.summary: Political journalism's focus on the "Game Story" hinders understanding of the political world. This story prioritizes politicians' strategies and actions within a competitive game, neglecting policy substance, impact on citizens, and diverse perspectives. The author argues this approach, often rooted in objective journalism, results in a detached view that makes politics less accessible and more alienating. The solution proposed is a journalism that interprets political struggles, examines policy impacts, and centers on citizens, ultimately fostering a better understanding of the issues. This shift requires a more engaged journalism that helps citizens understand the world, rather than simply reporting on the political game.
RECORD-00609.quote: If you’re still reporting on the game, you’re still part of the problem. Because the game is not the substance. And the substance is what matters.
concepts: Horse-race journalism
Church of the Savvy
View from Nowhere
The Production of Innocence
RECORD-00609.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00623.summary: Between 1980 and 2008, a Pew Research Center report indicated a significant decline in the number of journalists, despite an increase in the number of political campaigns and events to cover. While the number of newspapers decreased, the average size of newspapers increased. Simultaneously, the number of accredited reporters covering conventions and in the White House and Capitol Hill significantly grew. Further research from the Annenberg Public Policy Center revealed a strong focus on campaign process, strategy, and "horse race" elements in news coverage, which overshadowed substantive issues. This shift toward analyzing a candidate's motives and strategies, described by Thomas Patterson, has further contributed to the broken state of political coverage. The core issue lies in the fact that fewer journalists must cover more events, leading to a focus on easily reported aspects like strategy and process, ultimately diminishing the emphasis on policy and substance.
RECORD-00623.quote: American political journalism is broken. It is good at some things, like telling us who’s winning and losing the race, but it is failing at one of its most important assignments: helping the public to understand the nation’s problems and the choices we face in addressing them.
concepts: Church of the Savvy
Horse-race journalism
RECORD-00623.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00648.summary: The author identifies three crucial kinds of context often missing in discussions of intellectual history, using Hayek's work as a case study. The first is the specific problem Hayek was addressing, which was how a society of free individuals could achieve optimal resource allocation despite dispersed knowledge. Second, the relevant intellectual tradition, namely the Austrian school, and Hayek's engagement with Mises and subjectivism, is essential. Lastly, the context of the arguments within Hayek's essay "Economics and Knowledge" itself clarifies his focus on coordinating decentralized knowledge through the market process rather than individual plan optimization. The author emphasizes that these contextual elements shape the interpretation of Hayek's ideas, differentiating them from the concerns of others like Robbins.
RECORD-00648.quote: When you’re an expert in a field, you forget what it was like to be a novice. You forget that the things that seem obvious to you are not at all obvious to someone who’s just starting out. And so you fail to explain the context of your requests.
concepts: False balance
RECORD-00648.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00639.summary: The author recounts a past Twitter mistake stemming from frustration during a job search. They accidentally linked a negative tweet to a resume-related article instead of the intended social media blog post, leading to unintended agreement and embarrassment after it went viral. The author emphasizes the importance of carefully reviewing tweets, especially those with links, and avoiding tweeting while angry.
RECORD-00639.quote: What I failed to realize is that my attempt to be helpful was just another form of condescension.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience
Audience atomization overcome
Mindcasting
RECORD-00639.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00074.summary: NYU's Studio 20 journalism program, directed by Jay Rosen, represents a departure from traditional journalism education. Instead of focusing on training students for specific roles in a stable media industry, Studio 20 emphasizes innovation and collaboration with major media partners on real-world projects. The program's three studios culminate in individual projects where students work with media organizations on public projects, providing valuable experience and potentially leading to job opportunities. While acknowledging the need for further skill development, particularly in data visualization and programming, the program is lauded for its flexibility and adaptability to the evolving media landscape.
RECORD-00074.quote: Studio 20 acknowledges this reality and seeks to find hope and opportunity in a situation that can seem bleak to those considering — or already in the midst of — a career in journalism.
concepts: Audience atomization overcome
The People Formerly Known as the Audience
RECORD-00074.author: Corbin Hiar

RECORD-00077.summary: NPR's media correspondent David Folkenflik interviews Jay Rosen about his concept of the "view from nowhere," which Rosen argues is the media's attempt to appear unbiased and trustworthy. Rosen believes journalists should reveal their backgrounds and convictions to build trust with the public. This contrasts with the traditional view of impartiality, as advocated by Leonard Downie, former executive editor of The Washington Post, who believes that journalists should strive for objectivity and avoid partisanship.
RECORD-00077.quote: The view from nowhere - that's the name Rosen gives to what he says is the media's true ideology, a way of falsely advertising that they can be trusted because they don't have any dog in the fight.
concepts: View from Nowhere
RECORD-00077.author: David Folkenflik

RECORD-00599.summary: Analysis of emerging digital journalism trends and technology impact on news.
RECORD-00599.quote: Technology will reshape news gathering and distribution.
concepts: Digital Journalism
Technology Impact
Future of News
RECORD-00599.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00647.summary: A recurring pattern in responses to criticism involves claiming the critic "just doesn't get it," often employed to avoid directly addressing the substance of the critique. This tactic is frequently used by politicians, pundits, and online commentators. The author identifies two potential causes: a simple misunderstanding stemming from differing ideas of clarity, or deliberate vagueness in the initial statement. The latter allows speakers to maintain flexibility, deflecting criticism by claiming misinterpretation or difficulty on the critic's part, enabling them to present ideas without the risk of being clearly contradicted. The author observes this trend particularly in online discussions about social media, blogging, and politics, prompting an examination of its frequent use.
RECORD-00647.quote: This way of responding to critics seems to immunize Christianity against any rational criticism. For any objection, no matter how powerful, one can always draw a distinction that the critic has failed to draw.
concepts: The Production of Innocence
Church of the Savvy
RECORD-00647.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00638.summary: The author discusses the Transportation Security Administration (TSA), acknowledging its existence for security but criticizing its ineffectiveness and infringement on civil liberties. After widespread complaints, major news outlets and even the White House are now addressing the issue, offering a glimmer of hope for positive change.
RECORD-00638.quote: What Howard Kurtz is doing is playing the classic apologist’s role. He’s taking the government’s side in what is a very real controversy, and he’s doing it by taking down the very reporters who finally got the story right.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience
Mindcasting
RECORD-00638.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00643.summary: The author recounts a conversation about Thomas Frank's criticism of consumer culture, specifically citing an article on the film Fight Club as an example. Initially believing Frank wrote the article, the author later learned it was actually written by Andrew Potter. The author, a long-time admirer of Frank, was surprised and corrected their friend. The post acknowledges the mistake, credits Andrew Potter for the article, and provides a link to it.
RECORD-00643.quote: There is a good deal more to this story than Frank chooses to tell.
concepts: Mindcasting
RECORD-00643.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00076.summary: This Q&A explores the concept of the "View from Nowhere" in journalism, a term borrowed from philosopher Thomas Nagel. Rosen critiques its unearned authority in American newsrooms, arguing it encourages bad habits and hinders trust. He advocates for a pluralistic approach, where journalists with transparent perspectives coexist with those adhering to impartiality.
RECORD-00076.quote: In fact, American journalism is dumber than most journalists, who often share my sense of absurdity about these practices.
concepts: View from Nowhere
RECORD-00076.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00650.summary: Many high school students lack even a basic understanding of fundamental concepts such as the Constitution, Bill of Rights, and scientific theories, according to the National Assessment of Educational Progress results. A significant percentage of students score below basic in U.S. History, Civics, and Science, indicating a failure to grasp essential knowledge. The author believes this lack of education harms both students and the country, hindering informed participation in democracy and the ability to critically evaluate information. Addressing this issue requires a renewed focus on educating youth to ensure a healthy and functional democracy.
RECORD-00650.quote: We are armed not with knowledge of things, but acquaintance with them.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience
The Citizens Agenda
Not the odds but the stakes
RECORD-00650.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00651.summary: The article explores how the definition of "media" is changing and the impact on those who work in journalism. As new forms of information dissemination emerge, like blogging and citizen journalism, the author questions the need for a new term to describe journalists who uphold traditional journalistic principles and work within established media institutions. The author proposes calling these individuals "traditional journalists" or "professional journalists" to differentiate them within the evolving media landscape and acknowledge their continued significance.
RECORD-00651.quote: The people formerly known as the audience are those who were on the receiving end of a media system that ran one way, in a broadcasting pattern, with high entry fees and a few firms competing to speak loudly while the rest of the population listened in isolation from one another— and who today are not in a situation like that at all.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience
RECORD-00651.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00193.summary: This article proposes a "Citizen's Agenda" approach to campaign coverage, arguing that journalists should prioritize voters' concerns rather than focusing solely on the "horse race." The author outlines a ten-step process for creating and implementing this agenda, involving extensive community engagement, feedback loops, and prioritizing voters' questions in campaign reporting. The author contends that this approach improves the quality of political discourse and counters the negative aspects of typical election coverage, even acknowledging potential conflict with candidates who might resist this approach.
RECORD-00193.quote: What does the electorate want the candidates to be discussing as they campaign for votes in this year’s election?
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience
Horse-race journalism
The Citizens Agenda
RECORD-00193.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00325.summary: This article analyzes the Wikileaks release of the Afghanistan war logs, focusing on Wikileaks' strategy of releasing documents to select major newspapers while simultaneously posting them online. Rosen discusses the implications of Wikileaks' stateless nature and its challenge to traditional notions of journalistic verification and the power dynamic between the state, the press, and a new type of non-state media organization. He also explores the potential for large-scale revelations to generate surprisingly muted public reactions, suggesting a cognitive dissonance in how we expect investigative journalism to impact public discourse and policy.
RECORD-00325.quote: We tend to think: big revelations mean big reactions. But if the story is too big and crashes too many illusions, the exact opposite occurs.
concepts: Verification in reverse
The People Formerly Known as the Audience
The People Formerly Known as the Audience
RECORD-00325.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00580.summary: This article responds to Jay Rosen's advice for journalists, largely agreeing with his emphasis on transparency and accountability but adding considerations about judgment and the limits of self-disclosure. The author argues that while journalists should strive for transparency and avoid opacity as a tool of power, they must also recognize trade-offs and acknowledge the complexities of personal bias.  The author questions the feasibility and value of extensive personal ideological disclosure, suggesting that a journalist's body of work should speak for itself and that excessive self-reflection can detract from journalistic practice.
RECORD-00580.quote: I don't like people who lie, cheat, or steal, or who dissemble for the sake of acquiring or using power, or who think narrowly about everything rather than broadly; who hold fast to dogma; who are quick to condemn those who refuse to condemn.
RECORD-00580.author: Marc Ambinder

RECORD-00376.summary: This article argues that journalistic objectivity, as traditionally practiced, is a form of persuasion designed to build trust by appearing unadorned and fact-based.  However, this approach, characterized by phrases like “just the facts,” is inherently flawed because all journalism involves judgment. The author proposes shifting away from the "View from Nowhere" toward greater transparency and a plurality of approaches, allowing journalists to express viewpoints while maintaining rigorous reporting standards. This shift is necessary to address declining trust in the press in the era of the internet and audience atomization.
RECORD-00376.quote: Reporting has authority because the reporter did the work.
concepts: He said/she said journalism
The Production of Innocence
Audience atomization overcome
View from Nowhere
RECORD-00376.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00420.summary: This article analyzes the Politico's reporting on General McChrystal's resignation, focusing on a paragraph initially published and later redacted, which suggested that beat reporters are less likely to report negatively on powerful figures to maintain access.  The author explores whether this observation is accurate and criticizes the Politico's decision to remove the paragraph and refuse to explain the edit, viewing it as a case of self-censorship to protect the reputation of beat reporters.
RECORD-00420.quote: I love a good conspiracy as much as the next guy, but this aint one.
RECORD-00420.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00519.summary: Jay Rosen responds to Marc Ambinder's critique of Rosen's article "Clowns to the Left of Me, Jokers to the Right."  Rosen clarifies his previous argument, emphasizing the distinction between journalism and ideological argument. He argues that while objectivity is not always achievable, journalists should strive for transparency and acknowledge when the truth is hard to ascertain. Rosen proposes a shift away from the 'view from nowhere' towards greater disclosure of journalists' perspectives, allowing readers to understand the context of their reporting.
RECORD-00519.quote: To stand back and look at a situation dispassionately is vital to accuracy, and in a sense to intellect itself. My almost foolproof measure of intellectual honesty is the ability to paraphrase the arguments of another such that the other recognizes his or her view in the paraphrase.
concepts: He said/she said journalism
The Production of Innocence
View from Nowhere
RECORD-00519.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00270.summary: This article challenges the common perception that the ideology of the US political press is easily definable as either liberal or conservative. The author argues that the press's apparent ideology is far more complex, shaped by factors such as journalists' cosmopolitanism, their pursuit of authoritative narratives that disrupt established viewpoints, and their inherent preference for 'good stories' which often highlight negative events. This results in a complex dynamic where journalists, while often personally liberal, generate narratives that are not consistently aligned with either the left or right. The author illustrates this complexity through analysis of journalist behaviors and the contrasting interpretations of their work from both sides of the political spectrum.
RECORD-00270.quote: In the sphere of deviance we find “political actors and views which journalists and the political mainstream of society reject as unworthy of being heard.” As in the sphere of consensus, neutrality isn’t the watchword here; journalists maintain order by either keeping the deviant out of the news entirely or identifying it within the news frame as unacceptable, radical, or just plain impossible…
concepts: View from Nowhere
He said/she said journalism
False balance
RECORD-00270.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00633.summary: The article discusses four main methods for scooping ice cream. It begins by acknowledging the common phrase "a scoop of ice cream" is not a perfect description due to the variety of scoop shapes and tools. The post will review these four ways, including the flat spoon scoop, and invites reader comments on other methods.
RECORD-00633.quote: We tend to venerate this kind of scoop, but the journalist is often just a transcription service.
concepts: Mindcasting
RECORD-00633.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00658.summary: David Gregory of MSNBC's Meet The Press faced criticism for not challenging a guest's inaccurate statement regarding the use of the reconciliation process. He admitted he was unaware the statement was incorrect and stated it is not his job to correct every factual error made by his guests. Gregory asserted his role is to elicit information and hold guests accountable, not to act as a fact-checker or editor. This approach has drawn comparisons to Fox News' practices.
RECORD-00658.quote: I think my job is not to say, ‘You’re not telling the truth.’
concepts: False balance
He said/she said journalism
View from Nowhere
The Production of Innocence
RECORD-00658.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00452.summary: Jay Rosen critiques CNN's prime-time programming, arguing that its adherence to the 'View from Nowhere' journalistic approach has failed to attract viewers.  He suggests that CNN's inability to connect with audiences stems not from a preference for opinionated news, but rather from a perceived lack of authenticity and engagement.  Rosen proposes an alternative lineup that rejects the pretense of objectivity and incorporates more engaging, opinionated programming.
RECORD-00452.quote: Maybe the View from Nowhere has failed, not because audiences want opinion rather than news but because the Voice of God isn’t as convincing as it once was.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience
View from Nowhere
RECORD-00452.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00489.summary: This article discusses the impact of the internet and social media on audience engagement, particularly at conferences.  The author, Jay Rosen, introduces the concept of "audience atomization overcome," describing how audiences, once isolated, are now connected horizontally (peer-to-peer) and vertically (to speakers/institutions). This interconnectedness significantly increases the risk for unprepared speakers, raising the bar for presentations. The article then provides ten strategies for avoiding negative feedback in this new context, emphasizing pre-event planning, audience engagement, and incorporating audience feedback during presentations.
RECORD-00489.quote: The people formerly known as the audience, once connected up to big institutions and centers of power, but not across to one another, have overcome their own atomization, which was a normal condition during the age of mass media. With the rise of social media and mobile devices they are now connected horizontally, peer to peer, at the same time as they connect vertically: to the news, the program, the speaker, the spectacle.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience
Audience atomization overcome
RECORD-00489.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00456.summary: This blog post outlines Jay Rosen's planned discussion points for a South by Southwest panel on the future of context in news.  He critiques the current news model's failure to provide sufficient background knowledge for readers to understand news updates, arguing that news organizations should prioritize explanation and context alongside episodic reporting.  Rosen proposes solutions like user-driven assignment desks for explanatory journalism and improved information tagging to connect individual news items to broader narratives.
RECORD-00456.quote: In order for the news to be informative people have to be informable, and simply delivering a stream of newsy updates won’t get us there.
concepts: Audience atomization overcome
The People Formerly Known as the Audience
RECORD-00456.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00654.summary: Legitimacy in journalism hinges on several key terms. Expertise is demonstrated through experience and knowledge. Independence, crucial for separating news from propaganda, requires journalists to avoid being swayed by external agendas. Objectivity involves presenting stories fairly and accurately. Transparency demands that journalists disclose their sources and methods. Accountability requires taking responsibility for errors and upholding ethical standards. Impartiality means treating all parties equally. Serving the public interest, by providing relevant information and promoting informed debate, is essential. Verification, through cross-referencing and fact-checking, is crucial for maintaining credibility, especially in the era of misinformation. These elements work together to ensure news is trustworthy and serves the public good.
RECORD-00654.quote: The primary obligation of a journalist is to the public.
concepts: View from Nowhere
False balance
Verification in reverse
The Production of Innocence
RECORD-00654.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00291.summary: This article details a collaboration between The New York Times and NYU's Arthur L. Carter Journalism Institute to create The Local: East Village, a hyperlocal news site. The project aims to innovate in hyperlocal journalism through a pro-am model, utilizing NYU students, faculty, and community members to create content published on nytimes.com. The collaboration explores new models for funding and community engagement in local news, leveraging resources from both institutions while acknowledging the challenges of fair compensation and community relations.
RECORD-00291.quote: Our aspiration is not to give birth to a replicable site—the East Village is not your typical neighborhood—but an outstanding one. Then we can say to the journalism world: go ahead, steal some of our best ideas.
concepts: Audience atomization overcome
The People Formerly Known as the Audience
RECORD-00291.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00388.summary: This article critiques a New York Times article about the Tea Party movement.  The author, Jay Rosen, focuses on the Times' description of a 'narrative of impending tyranny' within the movement.  He questions the Times' failure to assess the factual basis of this narrative, arguing that its omission stems from a journalistic pursuit of 'innocence'—a desire to appear detached and non-ideological—which compromises the accurate portrayal of political reality. Rosen argues this 'quest for innocence' leads to a distorted representation of events, prioritizing perceived neutrality over factual verification and contributing to a broader problem of deficient political journalism.
RECORD-00388.quote: The quest for innocence in political journalism means the desire to be manifestly agenda-less and thus “prove” in the way you describe things that journalism is not an ideological trade. But this can get in the way of describing things!
concepts: He said/she said journalism
View from Nowhere
The Production of Innocence
RECORD-00388.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00659.summary: When considering the wisdom of crowds, it's crucial to avoid blanket statements and recognize the nuanced nature of crowd behavior. It's essential to reject the notion that all crowds or their decisions are inherently wise or always wrong. Factors like emotion, misinformation, and groupthink can sway crowds. Individuals shouldn't automatically assume they are correct when disagreeing with a crowd, nor should they always go against the crowd. There are varying types of crowd wisdom, and the ability to discern when a crowd is wise isn't always obvious. Learning from crowds, even "dumb" ones, is possible, and blindly following or rejecting the crowd should be avoided. The key lies in understanding when and what aspects of crowd behavior should be rejected.
RECORD-00659.quote: When you’re thinking about whether to trust a crowd, the question isn’t whether you believe in the wisdom of crowds or not; the question is, are the conditions right for the crowd to be wise?
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience
RECORD-00659.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00652.summary: The author expresses dissatisfaction with the New York Times paywall, noting that it is easily bypassed by clicking a link, unlike the Wall Street Journal's paywall. The author, while supporting the NYT's right to generate revenue, questions the effectiveness of a paywall that can be circumvented. They suggest the paywall might serve different purposes, such as targeting a specific audience or encouraging subscriptions to RSS feeds, and propose that the NYT clarify its intent. The author ultimately believes the NYT should either fix its paywall to prevent access via links or be transparent about its function.
RECORD-00652.quote: As long as you click a link from another site, the paywall disappears.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience
Parity Product
RECORD-00652.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00653.summary: The author finds Sunday talk shows frustrating due to their format, repetitive political guests, and focus on Washington D.C. Their simple fix involves changing the format to feature one non-politician guest for a one-on-one interview followed by a round table discussion with experts, eliminating politicians. The author suggests moving the show's location out of Washington D.C. to reflect the country better and broadcasting it throughout the week on various platforms to reach a wider audience. These changes aim to make the shows more engaging and informative by focusing on issues rather than political maneuvering.
RECORD-00653.quote: When a guest tells a lie or misrepresents the truth, a giant “bullshit” graphic should flash on the screen.
concepts: Horse-race journalism
Church of the Savvy
The Citizens Agenda
RECORD-00653.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00656.summary: Jay Rosen's checklist offers a framework for ethical journalism, focusing on the impact of actions rather than perfect moral behavior. The checklist, developed for students and newsrooms, comprises eight key components: transparency regarding methods and motives; admitting and correcting mistakes; involving the community in newsgathering; showing empathy and humanity towards subjects; actively listening to audiences and sources; ensuring fairness and proportionality in reporting; practicing humility and self-doubt; and demonstrating courage. These principles aim to guide journalists in adapting their ethical practices amidst changes in the field, encouraging accountability and a rational, transparent approach to reporting.
RECORD-00656.quote: If you were on the receiving end of the story you are reporting and writing, would you feel that you were being treated fairly?
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience
Audience atomization overcome
The Production of Innocence
False balance
RECORD-00656.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00657.summary: The author reflects on a conversation about Obama's call for transparency and expresses skepticism about its feasibility given the political system's reliance on secrecy. They are concerned that the same people who initially praised Obama's transparency call are now defending the White House's spin tactics, questioning the Church of the Savvy's stance on the issue. The author believes that prioritizing the perceived greater good can erode transparency over time, making them distrustful of any statements made on the topic by this group.
RECORD-00657.quote: I suspect the press embraces savviness because it makes them feel like insiders. The rest of us may believe a candidate when he says he will do something, but they know better. They’ve seen it all before.
concepts: Church of the Savvy
The Production of Innocence
RECORD-00657.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00655.summary: The Republican Party in Texas faces internal challenges, despite its history of electoral success. The party struggles with a primary problem, as run-offs often push the party toward extremes, silencing moderate voices. Moderate Republicans sometimes vote in the Democratic primary. However, the party's conservative principles, like low taxes and regulations, remain popular, and the state's growing population brings in new conservative voters. The Republican Party can succeed in Texas by addressing the primary issues and re-integrating moderate viewpoints. The future of the party in Texas is promising, but requires effort.
RECORD-00655.quote: What you are witnessing is the de-bugging of the software that runs in the heads of Washington journalists. The software is called, “the view from nowhere.”
concepts: Church of the Savvy
Horse-race journalism
RECORD-00655.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00585.summary: The author critiques Jay Rosen's optimistic view on the decline of "he said, she said" journalism.  While acknowledging that sophisticated journalists recognize the flaws of false balance, the author argues that economic pressures in the media industry, including job cuts and the loss of specialized journalists, make the lazy shortcut of "he said, she said" reporting even more prevalent. The author concludes that the blogosphere's ability to counteract this trend is limited due to the underlying economic realities of the media business.
RECORD-00585.quote: There's a reason the critique of false "balance" emerged, in significant part, from the science journalism world. In CJR, I was very much channeling the complaints of many evolutionary and climate scientists, who were outraged by media coverage and continually pointed out that since there's no such thing as "balance" in science, reporting about science which employs such a paradigm often gets the story completely wrong.
concepts: He said/she said journalism
RECORD-00585.author: Chris Mooney

RECORD-00387.summary: This article critiques the "he said, she said" style of journalism, arguing that it often fails to assess competing truth claims and instead offers a false sense of balance.  The author contends that this approach, while seemingly a quick and easy solution to reporting deadlines and the complexity of verifying information, ultimately hinders truth-telling.  The rise of the internet and readily available information sources have made this style of reporting increasingly untenable, as readily available evidence allows for a more nuanced and accurate presentation of facts, moving beyond a simple recitation of opposing viewpoints.
RECORD-00387.quote: “How much more evidence do you need?” is the kind of exasperation a lot of us have felt with what he calls “false balance,” which is another name for the pattern I’m describing.
concepts: False balance
He said/she said journalism
The Production of Innocence
Verification in reverse
RECORD-00387.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00606.summary: The blogosphere has changed journalism, moving it from a one-way communication system to one where many can speak and listen. The "he said, she said" reporting style, which quotes two sides without deeper analysis, is a weak approach because it often fails to understand the situation or provide genuine balance. This forces readers, the "active users" of the web, to independently evaluate the information and determine the truth, making the reporting style insufficient.
RECORD-00606.quote: It’s the lazy reporting of a dispute between two sides as if they have equal claims to the truth.
concepts: He said/she said journalism
False balance
The People Formerly Known as the Audience
Audience atomization overcome
RECORD-00606.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00628.summary: The "he said/she said" formula, common in news coverage, often presents conflicting viewpoints without adequate evaluation of their merit. While suitable for reporting negotiations, it can misrepresent issues where consensus exists on one side, such as scientific findings. This approach can be perceived as weak reporting by active online news consumers who are more engaged and critical of news construction. This active audience can see alternative ways for journalists to distinguish between credible and less credible claims, ultimately highlighting the need for journalistic judgment rather than merely presenting opposing arguments.
RECORD-00628.quote: You get trustworthy not by being “objective” but by showing your work.
concepts: He said/she said journalism
False balance
The People Formerly Known as the Audience
View from Nowhere
RECORD-00628.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00241.summary: The Huffington Post launches the Huffington Post Investigative Fund, a non-profit initiative funded by The Huffington Post and The Atlantic Philanthropies, aimed at producing investigative journalism. Jay Rosen, a senior advisor to the project, discusses its goals, including the use of open-source and distributed reporting methods, collaboration between professional and amateur journalists, and the importance of high verification standards. The Fund aims to 'report once, run anywhere,' making its content freely available for republication. The initiative sparks discussions about the future of investigative journalism, particularly its role in smaller communities.
RECORD-00241.quote: The announcement of its birth, along with the $1.75 million starter budget, is really the launch of a new Internet-based news organization with a focus on original reporting.
concepts: Parity Product
Audience atomization overcome
The People Formerly Known as the Audience
RECORD-00241.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00542.summary: This article curates a collection of essays and blog posts from March 2009, forming a 'flying seminar' on the future of news in the face of the newspaper industry's crisis.  The pieces explore various perspectives, from the sociological implications of the decline of the traditional press (Paul Starr, Yochai Benkler) to the internal struggles of news organizations (Clay Shirky) and the potential of new media ecosystems (Steven Berlin Johnson).  The authors discuss the changing production models of news, the potential for citizen journalism, and the challenges of adapting to a rapidly evolving media landscape.
RECORD-00542.quote: Society doesnt need newspapers. What we need is journalism.
concepts: The Production of Innocence
The People Formerly Known as the Audience
RECORD-00542.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00438.summary: This post reflects on Jay Rosen's appearance on Bill Moyers Journal, discussing his article "Audience Atomization Overcome" and the lack of coverage in the mainstream press.  Rosen highlights the discrepancy between the blogosphere's reception and the silence from the established political press, emphasizing his unique perspective gained from years of studying the national press. He expresses gratitude to Bill Moyers, PBS, and Glenn Greenwald for their support.
RECORD-00438.quote: I have been studying the national press since I received my PhD in 1986. This is the first time I have been able to unfold my own view of it on national television.
concepts: Audience atomization overcome
View from Nowhere
RECORD-00438.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00496.summary: This article reflects on the relationship between the presidency and the press, tracing its evolution from Theodore Roosevelt's proactive engagement with the media to George W. Bush's strategic distancing.  The author argues that Barack Obama's presidency presents an opportunity to redefine this relationship, advocating for greater transparency and a more direct engagement with the public, moving beyond the traditional model of a single interlocutor (the White House press corps) and the dominance of 'Big Media'.  The author emphasizes the need for Obama to actively shape the narrative, urging him to 'write it himself' – to control the information flow and actively engage with a broader, more diverse media landscape.
RECORD-00496.quote: What we should care about is not how many questions the press gets to ask at White House news conferences—a hapless metric—but how open to questions the Obama White House is in all the available ways: old, new and recovered.
RECORD-00496.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00340.summary: This article analyzes Daniel C. Hallin's model of the three spheres of journalism (consensus, legitimate debate, and deviance) to explain how the US political press operates. Hallin's model reveals how journalists implicitly define what constitutes acceptable political discourse, often marginalizing dissenting views and reinforcing existing power structures. The rise of the internet and blogging, however, allows like-minded individuals to connect, challenging the press's ability to control the narrative and define consensus, a phenomenon the author summarizes as “audience atomization overcome.”
RECORD-00340.quote: The ability to infect us with notions of what’s realistic is one of the most potent powers press and political elites have.
concepts: He said/she said journalism
Audience atomization overcome
The Production of Innocence
The People Formerly Known as the Audience
View from Nowhere
RECORD-00340.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00610.summary: The internet weakens the press's authority by fostering a connected public that can discuss, challenge, and create its own narratives about news.  This shift from an atomized audience to a connected one diminishes the press's control over opinion formation, the number of witnesses at events, definitions of the news, master narratives, framing, news filters, and professional ideology.  The press now faces competition from public discourse and alternative information sources, requiring it to justify its authority and position in the evolving media landscape.
RECORD-00610.quote: The audience has been de-atomized. And the press is still trying to figure out what to do about it.
concepts: Audience atomization overcome
The People Formerly Known as the Audience
View from Nowhere
RECORD-00610.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00616.summary: The internet fundamentally alters the authority of the press by dismantling audience atomization. Historically, the audience was isolated, reliant on the press to understand public sentiment and actions. The internet allows for public gatherings, comparison of ideas, the development of collective voices, and public action. This shift diminishes the press's exclusive ability to represent the public. The press retains authority, but must adapt by fostering public discourse, facilitating conversations, and partnering with the public in news production to regain its influence in the new environment.
RECORD-00616.quote: It was an authority founded on the public’s inability to speak.
concepts: Audience atomization overcome
The People Formerly Known as the Audience
RECORD-00616.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00437.summary: This article documents the author's process of writing a piece about his use of Twitter for the Chronicle of Higher Education.  It details his approach to explaining Twitter to a non-Twitter using audience, outlining the key aspects he plans to cover, and soliciting input from his readers on how they utilize the platform. The author frames his Twitter usage as a hand-built tipster network and seeks similar experiences from others to enrich his article.
RECORD-00437.quote: What I have so far: A dummy title. Why I Write 400 Words a Day and Put Them on Twitter. Whether that’s the actual title or not, it’s the question my piece must answer.
RECORD-00437.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00333.summary: This article discusses a shift in the Knight Fellowships at Stanford University, moving away from a model of general enrichment for mid-career journalists to one focused on journalistic innovation and entrepreneurship. The change is driven by the instability of the news industry, with newsrooms increasingly unable to absorb returning fellows or value their newly acquired knowledge. The new model emphasizes the creation of tangible, public goods by fellows, mirroring an open-source approach and aiming to increase the fellowship's impact on journalism beyond the individual level.
RECORD-00333.quote: The people who steer the Knight Stanford program decided it had to become more valuable to the social practice of journalism, worldwide. They don’t necessarily know how to do this, but they want to increase the supply of public goods the fellows create as a result of their year at Stanford.
concepts: Parity Product
The People Formerly Known as the Audience
RECORD-00333.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00329.summary: This article explores the evolving relationship between bloggers and journalists in the early days of the internet. Rosen argues that the distinctions between traditional journalism and blogging are less about inherent ethics and more about the different structures of closed and open editorial systems. He highlights the differences in production methods, gatekeeping versus filtering, and the nature of trust in each system. Ultimately, he contends that the success of blogging demonstrates that it has developed its own ethics based on the trust built between bloggers and their audiences within the open platform.
RECORD-00329.quote: If “ethics” are the codification in rules of the practices that lead to trust on the platform where the users actually are—which is how I think of them—then journalists have their ethics and bloggers have theirs.
concepts: Citizen Journalism
Press sphere
The People Formerly Known as the Audience
RECORD-00329.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00520.summary: John McCain's selection of Sarah Palin as his running mate is analyzed as a culture war strategy aimed at creating conflict with journalists and bloggers, exploiting the resentment narrative, and focusing on personalities rather than issues.  The strategy hinges on Palin's charisma and the ensuing controversy, leveraging both the intense support from social conservatives and the negative press coverage to generate a wave of attention and fundraising. The author notes the risks involved and the uncertainty of the strategy's success.
RECORD-00520.quote: At the center of the strategy is the flashpoint candidacy of Sarah Palin, a charismatic figure around whom the war can be fought to scale, as it were.
concepts: He said/she said journalism
The People Formerly Known as the Audience
RECORD-00520.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00288.summary: This article critiques a Mother Jones feature questioning whether Barack Obama's campaign rhetoric exaggerated its historical significance. The author challenges the feature's premise, arguing that there's no direct quote or evidence supporting the claim that Obama compared his campaign to past progressive movements. The author details their correspondence with Mother Jones editors, revealing a missing contextual speech excerpt that partially justifies the feature's framing, but still leaves crucial aspects unaddressed. The article highlights the dangers of inadvertently creating hype while attempting to debunk it and questions the journalistic rigor of the Mother Jones piece.
RECORD-00288.quote: There’s a moment in the life of every generation, when that spirit has to come through if we are to make our mark on history. And this is our moment. This is our time.
concepts: He said/she said journalism
The Production of Innocence
Verification in reverse
RECORD-00288.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00462.summary: This article analyzes the success of "The Giant Pool of Money," a This American Life episode explaining the mortgage crisis.  Rosen argues that the episode's effectiveness stems from its prioritizing of explanation over simply reporting facts. He contends that traditional journalism often fails to provide the necessary background context for understanding complex news events, leading to audience disengagement.  He proposes a shift in journalistic priorities, advocating for the creation of more explanatory pieces that serve as prerequisites for understanding subsequent news reports, thereby increasing audience engagement and comprehension.
RECORD-00462.quote: If explanation is required for information acquisition, then the explainer comes before the informer as a pre-requisite.
RECORD-00462.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00436.summary: This article analyzes Brian Ross's response to questions regarding ABC News's inaccurate anthrax reporting in 2001.  The author presents a fictional Q&A summarizing Ross's responses, highlighting inconsistencies and raising concerns about the network's handling of the situation, lack of corrections, and potential implications for the relationship between media, government, and the public. The piece also discusses the broader implications of the incident for journalism and its relationship with power in the post-Iraq War era.
RECORD-00436.quote: The watchdog press died under Bush. We may have a watchdog press again some day, it could be reborn. But it died. And really the only way we’re going to know that full story is through some kind of, almost like a media truth and reconciliation commission, which I have no hope for.
RECORD-00436.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00416.summary: This article details a coordinated effort by bloggers and journalists to hold ABC News accountable for its 2001 anthrax reporting, which falsely linked Iraqi involvement.  The author, Jay Rosen, and Dan Gillmor posed three key questions to ABC News regarding the sourcing and accuracy of their reporting, emphasizing the importance of transparency and accountability when confidential sources mislead. The response from ABC News, along with commentary from various journalists and publications, highlighted the ethical dilemmas surrounding confidential sources and the need for investigative journalism to correct the record in cases of significant misinformation.
RECORD-00416.quote: A substantially false story that helps make the case for war by raising fears about enemies abroad attacking the United States is released into public debate because of faulty reporting by ABC News.
concepts: The Production of Innocence
Verification in reverse
RECORD-00416.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00257.summary: This article explores the definition of citizen journalism, focusing on the author's concise definition: "When the people formerly known as the audience employ the press tools they have in their possession to inform one another, that’s citizen journalism." The author discusses various perspectives on the term, including those from bloggers and other media analysts, and highlights the implications for the traditional news media, suggesting that citizen journalism represents a shift in how information is created and disseminated, moving away from a model of the press as a singular information pipeline.
RECORD-00257.quote: When the people formerly known as the audience employ the press tools they have in their possession to inform one another, that’s citizen journalism.
concepts: Audience atomization overcome
The People Formerly Known as the Audience
Citizen Journalism
RECORD-00257.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00555.summary: This article contrasts two responses to the decline of traditional newspapers.  One is the curmudgeonly resistance of veteran journalists clinging to the past, exemplified by the hostile reactions to a young intern's positive assessment of her editor's restructuring plans. The other is a proactive approach, represented by the Tree House Media Project, which empowers journalists to become self-publishers and adapt to the changing media landscape.  Rosen argues that the future lies in embracing self-reliance and abandoning the 'mass' identity of traditional media in favor of more human-scale approaches.
RECORD-00555.quote: No longer does one need a printing press to publish, only a personal computer, an Internet connection and an idea.
concepts: Audience atomization overcome
The Production of Innocence
The People Formerly Known as the Audience
RECORD-00555.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00180.summary: This 2008 essay by Jay Rosen uses the metaphor of migration to describe the transformation of journalism in the digital age. Rosen argues that professional journalists, facing the decline of their traditional business model, must adapt to a new media landscape characterized by two-way communication, horizontal sharing, and the rise of citizen journalism. He highlights the challenges of this transition, including resistance from within the profession and the need to integrate professional and amateur journalism practices. Rosen uses the example of OffTheBus, a project he co-founded with Arianna Huffington, as an illustration of a distributed reporting model for campaign coverage.
RECORD-00180.quote: The land that newsroom people have been living on—also called their business model—no longer supports their best work.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience
Horse-race journalism
Audience atomization overcome
RECORD-00180.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00446.summary: This post updates the progress of Beatblogging.org, a project exploring whether beat reporters can improve their work by using social networks.  David Cohn, the original editor, has secured funding for a new project, spot.us, and Patrick Thornton has taken over Beatblogging.org.  The project will continue to profile beat reporters using networked approaches and collaborate with WiredJournalists.com to reach a wider audience of innovative journalists.
RECORD-00446.quote: Maybe a beat reporter could do a way better job if there was a ‘live’ social network connected to the beat, made up of people who know the territory the beat covers, and want the reporting on that beat to be better.
concepts: Audience atomization overcome
The People Formerly Known as the Audience
RECORD-00446.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00361.summary: This article details a collaborative project, the "McCain News Hunt," which utilized NewsTrust, a platform for rating and sharing news stories, and OffTheBus to crowdsource the best journalism about John McCain during a specific week. Participants rated 233 stories, resulting in a ranked list highlighting the top-rated pieces and demonstrating the potential of social media and collaborative filtering to improve news discovery and quality in a proliferating media landscape.
RECORD-00361.quote: The results aren’t spectacular or surprising, and I make no large claims for them. They do show that people really like accountability journalism and that Charlie Savage, now of the New York Times, wrote the most important McCain piece that week.
concepts: Audience atomization overcome
The People Formerly Known as the Audience
RECORD-00361.author: Jay Rosen and Gabriel Beltrone

RECORD-00529.summary: This article analyzes a case involving Mayhill Fowler, a citizen journalist contributing to OffTheBus, who obtained an off-the-record comment from Bill Clinton.  The incident sparks a debate about the ethics and implications of citizen journalism, particularly concerning transparency, the changing nature of 'off the record' interactions, and the relationship between professional and citizen journalists. The author explores the evolving media landscape and questions traditional journalistic practices in light of the increased accessibility of information and the blurring lines between professional and amateur reporting.
RECORD-00529.quote: Professional reporters are going to have to decide whether they want to view citizen journalists as unfair competition, which is one option, or as extending the news net to places that pro reporters can’t, won’t or don’t go, which is another—and I think a better—way to look at it.
concepts: Citizen Journalism
The People Formerly Known as the Audience
RECORD-00529.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00210.summary: This article analyzes Scott McClellan's tenure as White House press secretary, arguing that his role was not to communicate effectively but to actively frustrate and delegitimize the press. McClellan's ineffectiveness, far from being accidental, was a deliberate strategy – part of a broader 'Rollback' policy to diminish the press's influence and enhance executive power. This involved minimizing communication, refusing detailed answers, and promoting an environment of non-engagement to reduce the press's ability to hold the administration accountable.
RECORD-00210.quote: McClellan’s job was to contest or deny the ‘terrain of fact,’ the empirical evidence, as traditionally defined.
concepts: The Production of Innocence
False balance
Church of the Savvy
RECORD-00210.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00528.summary: This article analyzes Scott McClellan's post-White House reflections, connecting his experience as press secretary to a broader shift in White House communication strategies under the Bush administration.  Rosen argues that the Bush administration strategically employed non-communication and opacity, rejecting the traditional role of the press as an interlocutor between the presidency and the public. This departure from the Roosevelt-era model, where the president actively engaged with the press, represented a calculated effort to enhance executive power by controlling information flow and avoiding accountability.  McClellan's regret and public acknowledgment of his role in this strategy highlight the consequences of this approach and its ultimate failure in maintaining public support.
RECORD-00528.quote: The ruining of Scott McClellan was part of something way bigger, and to understand it we have to go back to the beginning of the White House press corps.
RECORD-00528.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00576.summary: This article discusses Clay Shirky's concept of "cognitive surplus," the vast amount of free time previously consumed by television, and its potential for productive online activity.  Rosen uses Shirky's ideas to explore the shift from passive media consumption to active participation and creation, exemplified by his daughter's blogging activities. He contrasts the passive nature of traditional media with the interactive possibilities of the web, highlighting the need for new media projects to utilize this untapped potential for social good.
RECORD-00576.quote: Someone working alone, with really cheap tools, has a reasonable hope of carving out enough of the cognitive surplus, enough of the desire to participate, enough of the collective goodwill of the citizens, to create a resource you couldn’t have imagined existing even five years ago.
concepts: Audience atomization overcome
The People Formerly Known as the Audience
RECORD-00576.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00199.summary: This article details the transformation of the Capital Times, a Madison, Wisconsin newspaper, from a daily print publication to a primarily online news outlet with two weekly print editions. The shift, driven by economic pressures and the changing media landscape, involves job losses, a move to a digital-first strategy, and a re-evaluation of the paper's role in the community. The author analyzes the challenges and potential opportunities presented by this transition, considering the competitive online environment and the paper's legacy as a progressive voice in Madison.
RECORD-00199.quote: The presses have stopped but the press goes on.
concepts: Audience atomization overcome
The People Formerly Known as the Audience
RECORD-00199.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00457.summary: This article explores the crisis facing newspapers due to the internet's disruption of their traditional business models.  Rosen discusses the challenges of transitioning from an advertising-subsidized model to sustainable alternatives, questioning whether the public good of quality journalism can be maintained. He examines various approaches, including non-profit models like ProPublica, innovative ventures like The Politico, and the potential for filtering and repackaging online content. The article also touches upon the inherent inefficiencies of advertising and the need for increased public understanding of the true cost of serious journalism.
RECORD-00457.quote: The traditional newspaper formula has been patently unworkable for years, but too many newspaper leaders don’t understand that.
RECORD-00457.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00449.summary: This article discusses the case of Mayhill Fowler, an Obama supporter and citizen journalist who reported on comments made by Obama at a fundraiser.  Her report, published on the Huffington Post's OffTheBus blog, was picked up by major news outlets but was subsequently downplayed by Meet the Press, leading to a discussion about the evolving role of citizen journalism in political coverage and the challenges faced by traditional media in navigating this new landscape. The article explores the blurred lines between citizen journalist, campaign supporter, and news reporter, highlighting the lack of established frameworks for understanding this emerging phenomenon.
RECORD-00449.quote: The issue is less the distinction between “citizen” and “journalist” and more whether the Founding Fathers ever contemplated such a distinction in the first place.A close reading of the First Amendment and centuries of legal precedent says “no.”
concepts: Citizen journalism
The People Formerly Known as the Audience
RECORD-00449.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00488.summary: This article analyzes the emerging conflict between liberal bloggers and mainstream media regarding their coverage of John McCain's presidential campaign in 2008.  The author questions whether a declared 'blogospheric war' against the media is truly underway, or if the situation is more nuanced and dynamic.  The piece examines the media's perceived favoritism towards McCain, the bloggers' strategies to counter this narrative, and the potential impact of McCain's unprecedented openness to press questioning on the campaign.
RECORD-00488.quote: This campaign is not going to be between the Democrats and the Republicans, said Philadelphias Duncan Black, who writes under the name Atrios and whose highly popular progressive political blog, named Eschaton, inspired the gathering of bloggers and political activists called Eschacon ‘08.
RECORD-00488.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00626.summary: The program features a discussion with media critic and NYU professor Jay Rosen about the current state of news and its role in a divided America. It highlights the business aspects of news in the digital age, while also acknowledging its importance as a public good. The conversation centers on the challenges facing journalism, including shrinking newsrooms, rising disinformation, and declining trust. Rosen advocates for a shift in journalistic approach, urging the press to move beyond objectivity and neutrality to actively defend democracy by calling out misinformation and supporting democratic norms. The discussion also includes the impact of AI on journalism, the future of local news, and the challenge of rebuilding public trust.
RECORD-00626.quote: The idea that there is this large, untapped audience of people in the middle who are just waiting for a news organization to come along and give it to them straight, that’s a fantasy.
concepts: View from Nowhere
Horse-race journalism
False balance
Not the odds but the stakes
RECORD-00626.author: Christopher Lydon

RECORD-00478.summary: This article analyzes the unusually positive relationship between John McCain's presidential campaign and the press corps.  The author argues that McCain's willingness to engage in extensive, off-the-record conversations with reporters, even when facing tough questions, cultivated a sense of rapport and trust, creating a 'reputational capital' that shielded him from harsher criticism.  The author contrasts this with other candidates' more guarded approaches, highlighting how McCain's openness, while potentially containing strategic elements, inadvertently humanized both him and the reporters, resulting in more favorable coverage. The article also explores whether Barack Obama should adopt a similar strategy.
RECORD-00478.quote: The currency in which reporters trade is questions actually answered, QAA. McCain simply realized that the QAA system allowed him to print money, as in: ask all the questions you want!And where does that currency go? Straight into Chuck Todd’s Presumptive Credibility Bank.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience
The Production of Innocence
RECORD-00478.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00238.summary: This post critiques CNN's Wolf Blitzer's analysis of Barack Obama's speech addressing the Jeremiah Wright controversy. Rosen argues that Blitzer's interpretation, focusing solely on political strategy, misses the speech's deeper message urging a transcendence of divisive political discourse and a more nuanced understanding of race. Rosen contrasts Blitzer's shallow analysis with the insightful observations of Greg Sargent and Charles Murray, highlighting Obama's direct challenge to the media's role in perpetuating a spectacle-driven, race-focused narrative.
RECORD-00238.quote: It is so far above the standard we’re used to from our pols… rhetorically, but also in capturing a lot of nuance about race in America.
concepts: He said/she said journalism
Church of the Savvy
The Production of Innocence
View from Nowhere
RECORD-00238.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00323.summary: This article critiques the prevailing notion of journalistic neutrality, arguing that it hinders effective political reporting and undermines democratic processes. It uses examples like Clark Hoyt's defense of the New York Times' neutrality, Josh Marshall's TPM's transparently liberal approach, and Walter Pincus' call for journalistic courage to illustrate the need for a more politically engaged and self-aware press. The piece emphasizes the importance of fairness over neutrality, advocating for transparency about reporters' political affiliations and a reevaluation of the power dynamics between the press and government, particularly addressing the legacy of controlled messaging started during the Reagan administration.
RECORD-00323.quote: “The biggest reason to go open kimono is that the present system does what journalism should never do: it perpetuates a lie.”
concepts: He said/she said journalism
The Production of Innocence
View from Nowhere
RECORD-00323.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00014.summary: The article analyzes instances where news organizations, particularly The New York Times and The Washington Post, engage in 'misguided contrarianism' by publishing provocative or seemingly iconoclastic pieces that ultimately serve to promote the paper's self-image rather than contribute meaningfully to public discourse. It critiques the pressure to 'find something' on all political candidates and the tendency to prioritize staff morale or economic concerns over journalistic integrity.
RECORD-00014.quote: The paper is not so much a paper anymore; it is itself a candidate.
concepts: False balance
He said/she said journalism
RECORD-00014.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00019.summary: The article analyzes instances where news organizations, particularly The New York Times and The Washington Post, publish controversial or seemingly contrarian pieces, suggesting that these actions are often driven by a desire to shape the publication's self-image as independent and iconoclastic rather than a genuine pursuit of truth or impactful journalism. The author critiques this 'misguided contrarianism,' arguing that it can lead to poor editorial decisions and a misreading of cultural politics.
RECORD-00019.quote: The paper is not so much a paper anymore; it is itself a candidate.
concepts: False balance
RECORD-00019.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00012.summary: Jay Rosen questions the New York Times' decisions to investigate Obama's drug use, Hillary Clinton's marriage, and John McCain's lobbyist ties. He argues that each story went "weirdly wrong" and asks Romenesko readers for insights into what might have been the common factors behind these editorial choices during the vetting process of presidential candidates.
RECORD-00012.quote: Each was part of the “vetting” ritual in which the press imagines itself asking the hard questions of candidates who would be president. Each has a touch of the bizarre to it.
concepts: Horse-race journalism
RECORD-00012.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00017.summary: Jay Rosen questions the New York Times' decision-making process in pursuing stories about Obama's drug use, Hillary Clinton's marriage, and John McCain's lobbyist ties. He notes that each story went "weirdly wrong" and asks for insights into what might be the common thread among these cases of questionable journalistic judgment.
RECORD-00017.quote: what is going on here? Anything in common among the cases?
concepts: He said/she said journalism
RECORD-00017.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00336.summary: This article is a distillation of a New York Times Q&A with readers regarding their explosive report on John McCain's involvement with lobbyist Vicki Iseman. The NYT defends its reporting choices, addressing concerns about anonymity, the inclusion of potentially unverified information about a romantic relationship, the timing of the story, and the potential impact on McCain's campaign. They maintain the story's accuracy and their commitment to thorough investigative journalism, despite the significant backlash.
RECORD-00336.quote: We publish stories when they’re ready. Period. No matter when we publish them people see dark motives.
RECORD-00336.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00343.summary: This article analyzes the New York Times' handling of a story suggesting John McCain had an affair. The author criticizes the Times' editors for lacking political awareness, failing to understand the potential consequences of their reporting, and clinging to journalistic codes that prevented them from recognizing the political realities of the situation. He argues that the Times' readers exhibited a more nuanced understanding of the political implications than the editors, highlighting a credibility gap between the newspaper and its audience.
RECORD-00343.quote: If a newspaper is going to suggest an improper sexual affair, whether editors think that is the central point or not, it owes readers more proof than The Times was able to provide.
concepts: The Production of Innocence
View from Nowhere
RECORD-00343.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00358.summary: This blog post analyzes the New York Times's reporting on John McCain's alleged affair, questioning the timing of the story in relation to the paper's endorsement of McCain. The author raises concerns about the reliance on anonymous sources, the potential impact on the 2008 election, and the broader implications for media ethics and the relationship between the newsroom and editorial page. The piece also highlights the ensuing culture war and the Times's discomfort with defending its journalistic choices in the court of public opinion.
RECORD-00358.quote: For the New York Times, self-confidence on ethics poses its own risks, as well.
RECORD-00358.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00011.summary: Jay Rosen critiques horse race journalism, arguing that the campaign media operates as a 'herd of independent minds' lacking a central direction or capacity to learn from mistakes. This mindlessness results in superficial coverage focused on predicting outcomes rather than understanding the stakes, leading to inaccurate narratives and a failure to inform the public effectively.
RECORD-00011.quote: Campaign reporters tend to be massively other-directed. The reality-check is what the rest of the press is doing.
concepts: Horse-race journalism
RECORD-00011.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00016.summary: Jay Rosen critiques horse race journalism, arguing that the media's focus on predicting outcomes and insider perspectives results in a "herd of independent minds" incapable of critical thinking or adapting to new information. He contends that this mindlessness leads to inaccurate and uninformative reporting, as journalists prioritize conventional routines over genuine insight and analysis.
RECORD-00016.quote: Campaign reporters tend to be massively other-directed. The reality-check is what the rest of the press is doing.
concepts: Horse-race journalism
RECORD-00016.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00271.summary: This article analyzes the contrasting views of the conservative elite and the conservative base regarding the media. While the base often perceives the press as monolithic, liberal, and against the Bush administration, key figures like Karl Rove and Dan Bartlett, having gained insider experience, recognize a more nuanced reality. They acknowledge the press's inherent desire for compelling stories and its oppositional stance towards power, irrespective of party affiliation. This divergence highlights a strategic utilization of the base's perception of media bias to serve political goals, while insiders operate with a more pragmatic understanding of journalistic motivations.
RECORD-00271.quote: The press is generally liberal, he argued, but “I think it’s less liberal than it is oppositional.”
concepts: Church of the Savvy
He said/she said journalism
False balance
RECORD-00271.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00295.summary: Jay Rosen argues that Scott McClellan's role as White House press secretary under George W. Bush was not simply to disseminate information, but to actively frustrate and belittle the press, hindering genuine communication and increasing the opacity of the executive branch. McClellan's actions, Rosen contends, were part of a broader strategy by the Bush administration to reduce constraints on presidential power and limit accountability through strategic non-communication, rather than outright lying or traditional spin.
RECORD-00295.quote: McClellan’s specialty was not lying, or the traditional art of spin, but what I have called “strategic non-communication.” Lying we understand; spin we have to come to grasp. Non-communication we still do not appreciate. Its purpose is to make executive power less legible.
concepts: Church of the Savvy
The Production of Innocence
False balance
RECORD-00295.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00383.summary: Jay Rosen announces the launch of Beatblogging.org, a project involving 13 news organizations and their reporters who will experiment with integrating social networks into their beat reporting.  The goal is to explore whether a collaborative, pro-am approach to journalism, using social networks to connect with experts and the public, can improve the quality and reach of beat reporting.  The project will run for a year, with participating organizations including the Houston Chronicle, Star-Ledger, Wired.com, and others, each focusing on a different beat.
