RECORD-00448.summary: This article is an interview with John McQuaid, a Pulitzer Prize-winning investigative journalist who left the Times-Picayune due to cost-cutting and the changing landscape of journalism.  McQuaid discusses his transition to online investigative journalism, reflecting on the limitations of traditional newspaper models and the potential of the web for in-depth reporting. He highlights the shift in access to information, the changing role of the reader, and the challenges and opportunities of adapting investigative journalism to the dynamic nature of the internet.
RECORD-00448.quote: Newspaper journalists watched the revolution unfold on their desktops along with everyone else, and rejoiced. But, of course, without knowing it, we were also watching our own relevancy decline.
RECORD-00448.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00205.summary: This article discusses the Polling Place Photo Project (PPPP), an open-source initiative aiming to document the American voting experience through citizen-generated photographs. The project, a collaboration between AIGA, Design Observer, and NewAssignment.Net, seeks to improve the accuracy and understanding of the voting process by supplementing traditional media coverage with firsthand visual accounts. It also serves as a test case for the feasibility and ergonomics of large-scale, volunteer-based, open-source data collection and social network reporting.
RECORD-00205.quote: The project’s goal, according to its designer and prime mover William Drenttel, is “an archive of photographs that captures the richness and complexity of voting in America.” A second aim is to “encourage research into how voting happens and how voting can be made easier, clearer, less confusing, more reliable.”
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience
Audience atomization overcome
RECORD-00205.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00186.summary: Canadian Prime Minister Stephen Harper's deliberate strategy to undermine the Ottawa press gallery is analyzed. Harper, mirroring George W. Bush's approach, aimed to diminish the press's influence by limiting access and promoting alternative channels of communication. This involved restricting press conference question selection, favoring one-on-one interviews with handpicked journalists, and utilizing alternative media like podcasts and websites to bypass traditional media filters. While initially met with a walkout by the press gallery, Harper's strategy aimed at 'de-certifying' the press, thereby weakening its ability to hold the government accountable. The article contrasts this with the relatively positive press coverage Harper received, highlighting the strategic nature of his actions rather than a response to actual grievances.
RECORD-00186.quote: Harper wanted to see if he could fundamentally change the relationship between his government and the people who cover it.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience
The Production of Innocence
View from Nowhere
RECORD-00186.author: Ira Basen

RECORD-00275.summary: This blog post discusses Sunlight Foundation's new project, "Find out if Congress is a Family Business," which uses a distributed reporting model to investigate whether members of Congress employ their spouses on their campaigns. The project highlights the potential of citizen journalism and networked tools to enhance transparency and accountability in government. The post also touches on broader themes in journalism, including the need for innovation, the challenges facing traditional news organizations, and the evolving relationship between citizens and the media in the digital age.
RECORD-00275.quote: “Members who hire spouses to work on their campaigns pay them from the campaign contributions they raise from special interests— in effect, allowing their political fundraising to add to their personal income,” said the press release from Sunlight.
concepts: Audience atomization overcome
The People Formerly Known as the Audience

RECORD-00539.summary: This article features a Q&A with Jay Rosen, discussing the role of newspapers in the age of online media and citizen journalism.  Rosen analyzes Bluffton Today, an experimental newspaper that reversed the traditional print-to-web workflow, highlighting its attempt at community-driven journalism. He addresses concerns about the lack of respect for online journalism compared to established media, arguing that the failure is not just suppression of truth but a failure of imagination and methodology within traditional journalism. Finally, he discusses challenges and safeguards for ensuring accuracy and preventing misinformation in open-source reporting models.
RECORD-00539.quote: The people formerly known as the audience (as I call them) are now a producer force to be reckoned with, and Big Media has just started that reckoning.
concepts: He said/she said journalism

RECORD-00107.summary: This text describes an early experiment in citizen journalism, NewAssignment.net, funded by Reuters. The initiative, spearheaded by Jay Rosen, aimed to collaborate amateur and professional journalists on investigative reports using open-source methods. The funding would support the site's first editor, with an anticipated launch the following spring. Blog community responses expressed excitement and optimism about the potential for this collaborative approach to transform journalism.
RECORD-00107.quote: What's more important is to help journalists figure out how to interact with the blogosphere--that big global, interactive, viral conversation about the things that matter to people.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience
RECORD-00107.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00010.summary: Reuters is giving $100,000 to NewAssignment.Net, an experiment in open source journalism where people collaborate peer-to-peer in the production of editorial goods. The money will underwrite the costs of hiring the project's first editor. The aim is to draw smart crowds into collaboration and get stories done that aren’t getting done now, pooling intelligence and dividing up the work. The project seeks a middle path between traditional journalism and new forms like blogging and social media, exploring ways to augment and accelerate the creation of quality journalism.
RECORD-00010.quote: Ultimately, journalism is about the story and the pursuit of truth; it is not about the news industry, a j-school or a traditional newsroom structure.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience
RECORD-00010.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00015.summary: Reuters is providing $100,000 to NewAssignment.Net, an experiment in open-source journalism. The funds will be used to hire an editor to oversee the pro-am collaborative reporting projects. The goal is to leverage the collective intelligence of the public to uncover stories that traditional media outlets miss, emphasizing the importance of collaboration between amateurs and professionals in journalism. The project aims to explore how the falling costs of collaboration online can enable original reporting.
RECORD-00015.quote: The voice of god is over in news
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience
RECORD-00015.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00326.summary: This article discusses the Sunlight Foundation's initiatives to promote citizen journalism and increase government transparency. It highlights projects like Exposing Earmarks and the Political Transparency Project, which utilize citizen volunteers to investigate and report on government activities. The author explores the potential of the internet to empower citizens as watchdogs, while acknowledging the challenges and risks associated with amateur journalism.
RECORD-00326.quote: The internet, and the platforms it provides, has revealed a much richer, more imaginative, eccentric, and curious populace than popular culture portrays.

The People Formerly Known as the Audience

The post also highlights the importance of ease of use, clear assignments, and managing user expectations for the success of such collaborative projects, while acknowledging uncertainties about its viability.

The project uses a networked journalism model, combining professional journalists with citizen participation to investigate and report on government earmarks. The author analyzes the project's successes and challenges, including its slow start and questions about its political neutrality, highlighting the evolving nature of pro-am journalism and the complexities of citizen engagement in investigative reporting.
RECORD-00348.quote: This is networked journalism (professionals and amateurs working together to get the real story) beginning to come of age, and it’s very much in the spirit in my initiative NewAssignment.Net.

RECORD-00314.summary: This article responds to critiques of the author's proposed NewAssignment.Net, a platform for collaborative journalism funded by users and donors. Critics raise concerns about the feasibility of user-funded stories, the potential for ideological bias, and the challenges of balancing user input with editorial control. The author addresses these concerns by highlighting the role of editor reserve funds, the importance of establishing trust between editors and users, and the flexibility of the funding model. He also discusses the need for transparency and the possibility of incorporating other funding streams, such as advertising and syndication.
RECORD-00314.quote: The heart and soul is the connection, or bond, between a New Assignment editor and the community of users drawn to an editor’s portion of the site because they can participate in the coming together of important stories.

RECORD-00231.summary: Paul Bass recounts his experience transitioning from traditional corporate journalism to founding the online, non-profit New Haven Independent. He details the challenges and rewards of this shift, emphasizing the increased reader engagement, interactive elements, and the return to a mission-driven approach to local news reporting. The article highlights the limitations of corporate media and the potential of a non-profit, community-focused model for online news.
RECORD-00231.quote: I’ve concluded that, yes, most conventional journalists can make the leap into the future of community journalism. They’ll be excited to discover that they can return to the mission that brought them to the business in the first place, while finding new ways to work alongside readers to report the news and rebuild a civic dialogue.
concepts: Audience atomization overcome
The People Formerly Known as the Audience

RECORD-00303.summary: This satirical piece critiques mainstream journalism's self-congratulatory pronouncements about its supposed dominance over blogging. Rosen argues that journalists' attempts to incorporate blogging techniques are superficial and fail to capture the essence of what makes successful blogs thrive: passion, irreverence, consistent engagement, and genuine interest in the online conversation. He uses examples of prominent journalists abandoning their blogs and the lack of engagement from established news organizations' blogs to support his claim, highlighting the persistent gap between professional journalism's rhetoric and its actual practice in the digital space. The author concludes with observations about the poor competitive response of mainstream media to the challenges presented by online platforms and blogs.
RECORD-00303.quote: It would do us all good if the pros would stop predicting the demise of blogging, and get busy learning to use blogging in their reporting.
concepts: Parity Product
The People Formerly Known as the Audience
RECORD-00303.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00375.summary: This article is a response to Nicholas Lemann's critique of citizen journalism, "Amateur Hour."  Rosen largely agrees with Lemann's concerns about the quality and reliability of citizen journalism but argues against a simplistic dichotomy between professional and amateur journalism. He emphasizes the historical continuity between blogging and earlier forms of citizen journalism and suggests that a more nuanced understanding is needed, recognizing both the potential and limitations of both professional and citizen journalism. Rosen also highlights the challenges of funding and sustaining high-quality citizen journalism initiatives, like his own New Assignment.Net.
RECORD-00375.quote: Journalism is enmeshed with and supported by the media, but has an older and more important purpose.
concepts: He said/she said journalism

The People Formerly Known as the Audience
RECORD-00375.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00422.summary: This article discusses the potential challenges and benefits of NewAssignment.Net, a platform for crowdsourced journalism funding.  The central argument revolves around the crucial role of skilled editors in maintaining journalistic integrity and independence despite funding from interested parties.  Concerns about donor influence, the potential for biased reporting, and the reliability of crowd-sourced information are addressed, with the author emphasizing the importance of a strong editorial process and reserve funds to mitigate these risks.  The success of the platform hinges on the ability of editors to cultivate a network of reliable supporters, navigate conflicting interests, and maintain editorial control despite funding pressures.
RECORD-00422.quote: “The editor’s job at New Assignment is going to be as much about managing online community as about assigning stories, editing copy and mentoring reporters,” Scott writes. “That’s a demanding, but certainly not impossible, pile of responsibilities.”
concepts: Parity Product
The People Formerly Known as the Audience

RECORD-00537.summary: This article proposes NewAssignment.Net, a non-profit platform aiming to fund high-quality, original reporting through donations.  It leverages open-source methods, allowing for public participation in developing and refining story assignments before professional journalists are contracted to complete the work. This model aims to address the funding crisis in journalism by directly connecting interested citizens with investigative reporting projects, bypassing traditional media outlets. The platform intends to produce original journalism through collaboration between professional journalists and citizen contributors, and addresses funding challenges faced by the news industry.
RECORD-00537.quote: Journalism has always been subsidized, whether by the pure commerce of classified ads or the mass media monopoly of the old network newscasts.
concepts: Audience atomization overcome
The People Formerly Known as the Audience
RECORD-00537.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00377.summary: This article critiques a Fortune magazine column by Justin Fox that argues publicly traded corporations are the best ownership model for newspapers.  Rosen contends that Fox's assertion is based on a misrepresentation of prevailing wisdom within the newspaper industry. He argues that Fox presents a fact-free observation, lacking quotes, examples, or links to support his claim that the industry universally believes local ownership is the solution to its problems. Rosen counters with numerous quotes from various journalists and commentators showing a much more nuanced and cautious perspective on local ownership, highlighting the lack of evidence for Fox's sweeping conclusion.
RECORD-00377.quote: There’s an upside, there’s a downside to local ownership. Reasons to be hopeful, reasons to be wary.
RECORD-00377.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00286.summary: This article analyzes the intense backlash against the New York Times's publication of stories revealing secret government programs related to tracking global bank transfers and the war on terror. The author examines the legitimacy of the press in the face of government secrecy, the debate over journalistic ethics in covering classified information, and the political motivations behind the attacks on the press, connecting them to a broader strategy by the Bush administration to roll back the press's influence and expand executive power. The author also discusses the inadequacy of simple formulas like 'when in doubt, publish' and the lack of effective responses from journalism educators.
RECORD-00286.quote: Precisely because no one elected the press it must find other means of securing its legitimacy. These are inevitably political in nature; they involve persuasion and “public opinion” as well as the protections of law.
concepts: View from Nowhere
False balance
RECORD-00286.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00593.summary: This article discusses two prominent issues in journalism: the challenges of journalists' social media use and the impact of Google's AI on news traffic.  It uses the example of Terry Moran's dismissal from ABC News for a critical tweet about Stephen Miller and Trump to illustrate the complexities of social media policies for news organizations. The piece also addresses Google's AI-powered search results significantly reducing traffic to news websites, suggesting that news organizations need to cultivate direct relationships with their audiences through subscriptions and newsletters to counteract this trend. Finally, it acknowledges the retirement of media critic Jay Rosen from NYU.
RECORD-00593.quote: In networked journalism, the public can get involved in a story before it is reported, contributing facts, questions, and suggestions.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience
RECORD-00593.author: Jeff Jarvis

RECORD-00070.summary: This article, written from the perspective of 'the people formerly known as the audience,' announces their existence and the shift in power dynamics due to the rise of digital media. It emphasizes that the audience is no longer a passive recipient of information but active participants with the ability to create, share, and control media. The article challenges traditional media's perception of the audience as mere 'eyeballs' and asserts the audience's autonomy and ability to engage on their own terms.
RECORD-00070.quote: Once the users take control, they never give it back.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience
Audience atomization overcome
RECORD-00070.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00191.summary: This article explores the shift in power dynamics between traditional media and its audience, now empowered by new technologies and participatory platforms. The author argues that the audience is no longer passive, but actively involved in creating, sharing, and distributing information, thus challenging the traditional one-way model of media communication. This shift necessitates adaptation from traditional media organizations, who are urged to embrace collaboration and recognize the audience's agency.
RECORD-00191.quote: The people formerly known as the audience are those who were on the receiving end of a media system that ran one way, in a broadcasting pattern, with high entry fees and a few firms competing to speak very loudly while the rest of the population listened in isolation from one another— and who today are not in a situation like that at all.
concepts: Audience atomization overcome
Parity Product
The People Formerly Known as the Audience
RECORD-00191.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00607.summary: The author distinguishes between "people former" and "people latter" in journalism. People former are tied to traditional methods and identities, potentially threatened by the internet's changes, while people latter embrace new tools, focusing on effective information delivery rather than clinging to old forms. The core qualities of a good journalist remain consistent, but the most effective practitioners in the internet age are often those who are adaptable and not bound by legacy systems.
RECORD-00607.quote: We have things to say, and we have the means to say them. We are your new competition, your unpaid associates, your boss, your audience and your former audience. Live with it. Deal with it.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience
Audience atomization overcome
RECORD-00607.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00620.summary: The author addresses the audience, referring to them as the "People Formerly Known as the Audience". The audience is no longer just passive recipients of information but are now capable of creating, sharing, and engaging with media in ways not previously possible. This shift is a result of the internet, empowering individuals to become journalists, editors, and critics. The author emphasizes that the audience can now select, comment on, and remix content, participate in media operations, and are often knowledgeable and skeptical. The audience's expanded capabilities have fundamentally altered the relationship between media creators and consumers.
RECORD-00620.quote: They are citizens, and a citizen is not a consumer of news. Nor is a citizen a spectator. We are not just on the receiving end any more.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience
Audience atomization overcome

RECORD-00515.summary: Ken Sands, online publisher for The Spokesman-Review, discusses his newspaper's efforts to integrate user-generated content and social media into their journalism.  He argues that readers possess more knowledge than journalists and proposes experiments to leverage this collective intelligence, including webcasting news meetings, creating community blogs, and tapping into existing online fan networks.  Sands seeks collaboration and ideas from BloggerCon attendees to improve newsgathering and build a more sustainable business model.

The People Formerly Known as the Audience

It explores how the internet and distributed knowledge can be used to break news, focusing on collaborative reporting and citizen involvement. The author questions how to effectively utilize social networks, collaborative editing, and citizen journalism to produce reliable and impactful news stories while addressing concerns about accuracy, reliability, and potential manipulation by partisan opponents.

RECORD-00563.summary: This article analyzes the sale of the Philadelphia Inquirer and Daily News to a local ownership group, focusing on the implications of a “pledge” of editorial independence from the new owners.  The author explores the uncertainty surrounding the success of this experiment in local ownership, contrasting the perspectives of those who are optimistic about a potential break from traditional ownership models and those who are skeptical based on the history of the newspapers and the new owner's past.  The article highlights the importance of not knowing the outcome and the need for a truly experimental approach, acknowledging the potential for both success and failure.
RECORD-00563.quote: The future of democracy is going to depend on how well the country is informed about its problems.
RECORD-00563.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00468.summary: This article analyzes Tony Snow's debut as White House Press Secretary, contrasting his style with that of Scott McClellan.  Rosen argues that the Bush administration's approach to press briefings, characterized by limited transparency and control of the agenda, is inadequate for winning the 'war of ideas.' He proposes a dramatic increase in briefings, targeting diverse audiences including international and religious press, bloggers, and the general public, to counter the administration's perceived strategic communication failures and effectively engage in a global contest for public opinion.

concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience
The Production of Innocence

The transcript reveals challenges in managing the gaggle, including its unexpected early start and overcrowding, leading to adjustments in location and communication.  The Q&A session covers various topics, including the administration's credibility,  'Setting the Record Straight' strategy, international affairs, and an ongoing Justice Department investigation. Snow's responses often highlight his new role and limited knowledge of certain issues, while emphasizing his commitment to transparency and collaboration with the press.

RECORD-00239.summary: This article analyzes the abrupt resignation of CIA Director Porter Goss and its implications for the relationship between the Bush White House and the press. The appointment of Tony Snow as press secretary is interpreted as a shift away from this strategy, signaling a potential return to more conventional media engagement.  The author contrasts this approach with that of Theodore Roosevelt, who actively cultivated the press to enhance presidential power.  The article questions the effectiveness of the Rollback strategy and explores the broader implications of the White House's relationship with the media, particularly in the context of the 'War on Terror' and the battle for world opinion.

The author suggests that Waas's work represents a shift away from insider journalism and toward a more rigorous, fact-based approach.

Rosen critiques Keller's view that engaging with online criticism leads to unproductive "self-absorption," arguing that it reflects a misunderstanding of the dynamic nature of online conversation and a failure to adapt to the evolving power dynamics of the news media landscape. Rosen suggests alternative strategies for engaging with online criticism, proposing the creation of a Times blog dedicated to addressing editorial decisions and fostering more constructive dialogue.
RECORD-00476.quote: If you don’t explain yourself, you just invite others to do the explaining of you for you.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience
View from Nowhere
RECORD-00476.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00073.summary: This article presents an interview with Jay Rosen, a journalism professor, discussing the evolution from public journalism to citizen journalism and the potential of open-source journalism. He emphasizes that the web has shifted the debate, and journalists must adapt to the changing media landscape to remain relevant, sharing journalism with bloggers and developing a new collaborative relationship.
RECORD-00073.quote: All kinds of knowledge monopolies — and positions of authority based on them — are wearing away … [and] … the professionals who have gained control of institutions of various kinds — including politics — are not going to have that kind of control anymore.

RECORD-00345.quote: The blogospheric “market” should reward or punish behavior and let us develop consistent with the expectations and preferences of our readers.

The People Formerly Known as the Audience

The first installment examines the best blogging newspapers in the U.S., featuring a chart analyzing the state of newspaper blogging and interviews with key figures. RECORD-00256.summary: This article analyzes the Bush administration's, particularly Dick Cheney's, deliberate strategy of undermining the traditional relationship between the White House and the press. By ignoring established communication protocols and selectively releasing information, Cheney demonstrated a disregard for the press's role as a conduit to the public and a rejection of its perceived power. The author argues this represents a fundamental shift in the power dynamic, where the White House actively seeks to control the narrative and circumvent traditional journalistic practices, leaving the press weakened and unable to effectively hold power accountable.

concepts: View from Nowhere

RECORD-00198.summary: This article announces the launch of Blue Plate Special, a new online journalism project conceived by Jay Rosen. It will feature collaborative reporting on a monthly theme related to the intersection of the internet and journalism. The project is described as an experiment in online journalism, drawing inspiration from various successful examples of blog expansion, such as adding correspondents or creating spin-off sites. It also serves as a precursor to a planned overhaul of Rosen's PressThink website.
RECORD-00198.quote: Good information and multiple perspectives on a single theme— for now, that is the formula for a Blue Plate Special.
concepts: Audience atomization overcome
The People Formerly Known as the Audience
RECORD-00198.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00367.summary: Andrew Postman, son of Neil Postman, explores the continued relevance of his father's book, *Amusing Ourselves to Death*, twenty years after its initial publication. He argues that the book's critiques of television's impact on society remain strikingly pertinent in the age of the internet and ubiquitous technology, based on the reactions of college students assigned the book in their classes. While some students felt the book was outdated or offered no solutions, the overwhelming response indicated that Postman's observations about the trivialization of information and the dominance of entertainment continue to resonate.
RECORD-00367.quote: His questions can be asked about all technologies and media. What happens to us when we become infatuated with and then seduced by them? Do they free us or imprison us? Do they improve or degrade democracy? Do they make our leaders more accountable or less so? Our system more transparent or less so? Do they make us better citizens or better consumers? Are the trade-offs worth it? If theyre not worth it, yet we still cant stop ourselves from embracing the next new thing because thats just how were wired, then what strategies can we devise to maintain control? Dignity? Meaning?
RECORD-00367.author: Andrew Postman

RECORD-00269.summary: This article discusses an online roundtable on ethics and interactivity featuring Jim Brady (Washingtonpost.com), Jane Hamsher (Firedoglake), Glenn Reynolds (Instapundit), Jeff Jarvis (Buzzmachine), and Jay Rosen (PressThink). The discussion revolves around the Washington Post's handling of comments on their website, particularly after temporarily disabling them due to technical issues and a perceived lack of civility. The article highlights contrasting approaches to online reader engagement between the Washington Post and the New York Times, including the use of bylines linked to reporter email addresses, and the NYT's paywalled blog content. The differing viewpoints and heated exchanges during the roundtable, especially between Hamsher and Brady, underscore the challenges news organizations face in navigating online interactivity and reader engagement.
RECORD-00269.quote: Jim Brady told Dan Gillmor that more changes are coming at the Post site, once the Post fixes the problems it had last week.
concepts: Audience atomization overcome
The People Formerly Known as the Audience
RECORD-00269.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00469.summary: Jim Brady, then managing editor of washingtonpost.com, temporarily closed the comments section of post.blog due to abusive and uncivil comments targeting Deborah Howell, the Washington Post's ombudsman.  This decision sparked a debate about the balance between online transparency, reader engagement, and maintaining a civil online environment.  The article presents a Q&A with Brady, exploring the reasons behind the decision, the challenges of moderating online comments, and the broader implications for online journalism and public dialogue.
concepts: Audience atomization overcome
The People Formerly Known as the Audience
RECORD-00469.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00315.summary: Debra Galant, founder of the hyperlocal news blog Baristanet.com, reflects on the differences between her experience in traditional journalism (at The New York Times) and her current work in online, community-based reporting. She contrasts the institutional authority of established newspapers with the informal, sometimes irreverent, nature of her blog, highlighting the advantages of real-time reporting, direct audience engagement, and the focus on local, often overlooked, news stories that resonate deeply with the community. While acknowledging the challenges of maintaining a certain standard while fostering community discussion and dealing with criticism, she ultimately celebrates the unique opportunities and rewards of hyperlocal blogging.
RECORD-00315.quote: But bigger still is the shift from top-down control of media to control from the bottom, from the people, who are tired of corporate ownership and meddling and just want to be served, want to have a greater voice.
concepts: Audience atomization overcome
The People Formerly Known as the Audience
RECORD-00315.author: Debra Galant

RECORD-00494.summary: This article analyzes the media's misreporting of the West Virginia Sago mine disaster, specifically focusing on CNN's three-hour broadcast of false information that 12 miners were alive.  The author contrasts the actions of a local reporter who stayed at the official briefing room, finding no confirmation of the reports, with the actions of national news organizations that rushed to the church where families were gathering, relying on unconfirmed rumors.  The author criticizes CNN and other outlets for failing to properly verify information, highlighting the lack of confirmation from the rescue operation itself, and questions the media's assertion that their mistakes were unavoidable. The piece also explores the role of the public in evaluating the reliability of news in the age of instant communication.
RECORD-00494.quote: It is unacceptable to me that for three hours of live television, with our top talent presiding, we’ve got twelve men alive reported as truth, and we never saw those men, no ambulances for them ever moved, and we had no real confirmation.
concepts: He said/she said journalism
Verification in reverse
RECORD-00494.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00508.summary: This article analyzes the media's response to a false report that 12 miners had been rescued alive from a West Virginia mine.  It contrasts the differing responses of various news organizations to the erroneous information, highlighting the varied approaches to acknowledging mistakes and the importance of accurately reporting sources. The author emphasizes the need for a moral voice in admitting errors, prioritizing the reader's experience over internal journalistic justifications, and the crucial role of trust in the news-consuming public.
RECORD-00508.quote: Accuracy, which was achieved, is the more technical term, truth, which did not happen, is a moral category.
RECORD-00508.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00404.summary: This article analyzes the controversy surrounding the New York Times' reporting on warrantless NSA eavesdropping.  It focuses on the criticism leveled by the Times' public editor, Barney Calame, against executive editor Bill Keller's handling of the situation, particularly regarding the lack of transparency in explaining the delayed publication. The piece discusses the tension between the Times' commitment to transparency and the demands of investigative journalism, contrasting the perspectives of various journalists, bloggers, and commentators. It highlights the debate over the role of the public editor, the pressures of national security concerns, and the evolving relationship between the mainstream media and the blogosphere in the wake of the story.
RECORD-00404.quote: My point is, the independence rests mainly in the character of the person who holds the job.
RECORD-00404.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00005.summary: This article critiques Bill Keller's handling of transparency issues at The New York Times, specifically regarding the decision to publish a story about the Bush administration's secret lifting of limits on spying in the U.S. The author argues that the Times withheld key information about the story's background and the White House's attempts to suppress it, highlighting a lack of self-scrutiny and a resistance to engaging in open dialogue with its readers, despite internal recommendations to improve transparency.
RECORD-00005.quote: Heavyweights in journalism can’t figure it out. I certainly can’t. And the newspaper won’t say much.
concepts: View from Nowhere
RECORD-00005.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00300.summary: This article discusses the debate surrounding Dan Froomkin's White House Briefing column and whether its critical stance towards the Bush administration constitutes ideological bias or legitimate accountability journalism. Froomkin defends his approach, emphasizing his commitment to journalistic passion and accountability, regardless of the president's party. The piece also explores the tensions between traditional print journalism's emphasis on detachment and the more engaged style of online blogging, and the differing perspectives of print and online journalists at the Washington Post regarding this evolving media landscape.
RECORD-00300.quote: But its journalistic passion, not partisan passion. And what disturbs me is the suggestion that enthusiastically scrutinizing a Republican president is somehow de facto biased and liberal and therefore inadvisable for a reporter in a mainstream newsroom. I think thats toxic for the industry, and for democracy.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience
Verification in reverse
RECORD-00300.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00355.summary: This Q&A discusses the controversy surrounding Dan Froomkin's "White House Briefing" column on washingtonpost.com. The Washington Post's political staff expressed concerns that the column's title and presentation created confusion among readers about Froomkin's role as a commentator versus a reporter, potentially harming the paper's credibility. The debate centers on the line between opinion and news reporting in the online environment, the perception of Froomkin's column as having a liberal bias, and the broader challenges of maintaining journalistic objectivity in the age of the internet.
RECORD-00355.quote: What worries me is when I see headlines that suggest there’s a huge battle between the newspaper and the Web site.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience
Verification in reverse
RECORD-00355.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00525.summary: This article discusses the internal conflict at the Washington Post between its print and online newsrooms regarding the opinion column "White House Briefing" by Dan Froomkin.  The print side, concerned about perceptions of bias against the Bush administration, wanted the column's name changed, while the online side, led by Jim Brady, resisted, highlighting the tension between journalistic traditions and the dynamics of online readership and political pressures. The author uses this situation to argue for the benefits of maintaining a divided newsroom structure, allowing for a wider range of perspectives and a more dynamic approach to journalism in the digital age.
RECORD-00525.quote: What the brief struggle over White House Briefing showed me is the hidden advantages of a divided house.
RECORD-00525.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00312.summary: This article analyzes the controversy surrounding Bob Woodward's actions in the Valerie Plame leak investigation. It critiques Woodward's journalistic practices, particularly his close relationships with powerful sources and his seeming lack of critical analysis, arguing that his pursuit of access over truth hindered his ability to uncover the full story of the Bush administration. The piece contrasts Woodward's approach with the ideal of investigative journalism, highlighting the perspectives of various journalists and commentators, including David Broder, Eugene Robinson, Jane Hamsher, Nora Ephron, William Powers, and Joan Didion, to expose the limitations of Woodward's methods and the potential consequences of prioritizing access to power over investigative thoroughness.
RECORD-00312.quote: The best thing ever written about Woodward is nine years old, but its fundamentals still apply.
RECORD-00312.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00252.summary: This article analyzes Backfence, a hyperlocal, user-generated content website. While touted as a leader in citizen journalism, Backfence's slow growth and low user engagement raise questions about the viability of its model. The author compares Backfence to their own successful hyperlocal site, Baristanet, highlighting the differences in community engagement and content generation. The article discusses the challenges of attracting and retaining users in a user-generated content platform, particularly the difficulty of achieving a critical mass of contributors to generate a vibrant online community. The lack of organic local flavor and the uniform design are cited as potential impediments to attracting and engaging users.
RECORD-00252.quote: You cannot franchise Baristanet until the two of you learn to clone yourselves — which is why your site has heart and soul and wit and credibility and Backfence has venture capital. Yours is a community news site. Theirs is a business plan.
concepts: Audience atomization overcome
user-generated content
The People Formerly Known as the Audience
RECORD-00252.author: Judy Miller

RECORD-00500.summary: This article contrasts the failing "fortress journalism" model with the author's experience implementing a transparent newsroom at the Spokane Spokesman-Review.  The author argues that the traditional model, characterized by secrecy and a separation from the community, is failing, while transparency, including openness about mistakes and engaging directly with readers, enhances credibility and builds trust.  He cites examples from his career at various newspapers and draws on research from the ASNE credibility project to support his claim that a two-way flow of information, involving citizens in news production, is essential for the future of journalism.
RECORD-00500.quote: Transparency—which includes being open about mistakes—can kill rumors and conspiracy theories that breed distrust. It can soften criticism, or at least direct it to the appropriate targets.
concepts: Audience Engagement
Civic Journalism
Transparent Newsroom
User-as-Producer
Fortress Journalism
The People Formerly Known as the Audience
RECORD-00500.author: Steven A. Smith

RECORD-00614.summary: Jay Rosen discusses how a national political movement, particularly the Sinclair Broadcast Group, has built a "party-line propaganda instrument" using local TV stations. This involves Sinclair acquiring numerous local stations and replacing local news with national right-wing talking points, often delivered by anchors unaware of the content's origin. This strategy is seen as a radicalization tactic, injecting partisan views into local news and potentially undermining democracy by providing biased information. The interview touches upon the need for public awareness, FCC action, support for local journalism, and media literacy to combat this trend, emphasizing the role of a pro-democracy press in safeguarding democratic values.
RECORD-00614.quote: Because local TV news is still a trusted source of information for many people, Sinclair is able to inject its political propaganda directly into the bloodstream of local communities, disguised as news.
concepts: False balance
View from Nowhere
Parity Product
The Production of Innocence
RECORD-00614.author: Andrew O'Hehir

RECORD-00513.summary: This article reflects on the rise of citizen journalism in the mid-2000s, using the author's experience with her hyperlocal newsblog, H2otown, as a case study.  It contrasts the motivations and reward systems of citizen journalists with those of professional journalists, highlighting the entrepreneurial opportunities presented by the web for individuals to create local news sources.  The author also discusses the decline of traditional local newspapers and the resulting media void in many communities, proposing alternative business models for online news sources.
RECORD-00513.quote: I wanted to say to them, If you really want to do this, dont let a little thing like not getting a job stop you.
concepts: Audience atomization overcome
The People Formerly Known as the Audience
Citizen Journalism
RECORD-00513.author: Jay Rosen', 'Lisa Williams

RECORD-00298.summary: This article analyzes the controversy surrounding the Society of Professional Journalists (SPJ) awarding Judith Miller its First Amendment Award. The award was given for Miller's 85-day jail sentence for refusing to reveal a confidential source, but the article highlights concerns about Miller's questionable reporting on WMDs in Iraq and her handling of confidential sources, including a deal with Scooter Libby. The author explores the SPJ's justification for the award, emphasizing the advancement of a federal shield law as the overriding factor, despite concerns about Miller's professional conduct. The article also includes commentary on the implications of Miller's actions and the broader discussion around journalistic ethics and the use of confidential sources.
RECORD-00298.quote: Journalism has, as its core, the trust between reporters and editors, and reporters and the public. As that erodes, the whole enterprise starts to crumble.
concepts: He said/she said journalism
The Production of Innocence
RECORD-00298.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00552.summary: This article critiques the New York Times' handling of several major controversies, including the Judith Miller case, the Wen Ho Lee case, and the Jayson Blair plagiarism scandal.  Rosen argues that the Times repeatedly failed to learn from its mistakes, despite internal investigations and reports recommending increased transparency and engagement with critics.  He highlights the newspaper's reliance on confidential government sources, its reluctance to acknowledge errors, and its insufficient response to reader concerns, ultimately questioning the organization's commitment to journalistic integrity and accountability.
RECORD-00552.quote: They learn, we learn, and then maybe well all get to where we need to go wherever that might be.
RECORD-00552.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00250.summary: Jay Rosen announces a temporary hiatus from his PressThink blog to complete his book, "By the People." The announcement follows a series of seven posts criticizing Judith Miller and the New York Times' handling of her reporting, which are briefly summarized. Rosen expresses gratitude for the blog's readership and plans to return in December.
RECORD-00250.quote: Judith Miller may be the only investigative reporter alive who doesn’t care if you understand, because she does. She’s not aware of it when her stories do not add up. They cohere for her. In this sense she violates not the rules of journalism, but the reason we have it.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience
RECORD-00250.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00458.summary: This article analyzes the controversy surrounding Judith Miller's reporting on weapons of mass destruction in Iraq and her alleged security clearance.  The author questions whether Miller had a special security clearance that allowed her access to classified information beyond other reporters. He critiques the New York Times's response to inquiries about the matter, highlighting inconsistencies in Miller's statements and the lack of transparency from the newspaper. The author uses this case to discuss the role of bloggers in holding mainstream media accountable and the importance of journalistic transparency.
RECORD-00458.quote: What the New York Times has not figured out yet is that Judith Miller is an extreme example of the unreliable narrator. She increases our doubt in the story as she tells it.
RECORD-00458.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00338.summary: Andrew Heyward, President of CBS News, declared the "era of omniscience" over in mainstream news. He argued that news organizations must abandon claims to all-knowing objectivity and instead embrace the reality of multiple perspectives and a more authentic approach to reporting. This shift is driven by the empowered consumer and the rise of new media, forcing news outlets to adapt and acknowledge their limitations while maintaining accuracy and fairness. The article includes reactions from several writers who discuss the implications of this shift and its challenges for journalism.
RECORD-00338.quote: The strongest exemplars of mainstream commercial television news—60 Minutes, CBS News Sunday Morning, the network newscasts at their best—stand out not just by original reporting but also by avoiding these traps. And I’m convinced a consumer-empowered marketplace will reward authenticity over artifice.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience
View from Nowhere
View from Nowhere
RECORD-00338.author: Andrew Heyward

RECORD-00522.summary: This article critiques the New York Times' handling of the Judith Miller case, arguing that Miller's actions, framed as a First Amendment struggle, effectively hijacked the newspaper's decision-making process.  The author contends that the Times' prioritization of Miller's principles over journalistic ethics and factual accuracy led to a disastrous outcome, hampered by Miller's lack of cooperation and the leadership's failure to properly investigate and oversee the situation.  The author highlights instances of Miller's questionable behavior, including memory loss regarding crucial details and unwillingness to cooperate with colleagues.
RECORD-00522.quote: By taking Miller’s secret-keeping “into” itself the Times took on more and more responsibilities not to speak, not to publish, not to report, not to inquire. All this is deadly for a newspaper, and the staff knew it.
RECORD-00522.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00203.summary: This post analyzes Judith Miller's silence and lack of cooperation with the New York Times reporters investigating her role in the Plame affair. It puts forward a hypothesis that Miller will not fully cooperate and examines evidence from various sources to support this claim. The author also critiques the Society of Professional Journalists (SPJ) for planning to give Miller a First Amendment award before the full story is revealed.
RECORD-00203.quote: I am delighted that the contempt order has been lifted, and Judy is now completely free to go about her great reporting as a very principled and honorable reporter,” said Robert Bennett, Ms. Miller’s attorney.
concepts: Verification in reverse
RECORD-00203.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00258.summary: This article analyzes the New York Times's delayed reporting on Judith Miller's involvement in the Plame affair. The author speculates on the reasons for the delay, suggesting a combination of factors including the ongoing legal proceedings, the Times's own potential culpability, and the lack of cooperation from Miller herself. The author highlights the internal frustration and uncertainty within the Times newsroom, emphasizing the tension between the desire to publish a thorough investigation and the fear of publishing damaging information before all the facts are known. The piece ultimately questions the Times's handling of the situation and its implications for journalistic integrity.
RECORD-00258.quote: The New York Times is in a suspended state, editorially speaking. In fact, the entire organization—with the exception of a few lawyers, a few top executives, a few top editors, plus Jon Landman and his crew—is in the dark about Miller, uncertain of what a full investigation will find, unwilling to speak in the absence of knowledge now being gathered, fearful that the emerging story could be devastating.
concepts: The Production of Innocence
He said/she said journalism
False balance
View from Nowhere
RECORD-00258.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00493.summary: This article analyzes the New York Times's handling of the Judith Miller case, criticizing its lack of transparency and its failure to adequately explain its actions to the public.  The author points to inconsistencies in the Times' reporting, its delayed and inadequate explanations, and the contrast between its own actions and its usual standards of investigative journalism. The article highlights how the New York Times was scooped by other publications on crucial details of the Miller case,  raising concerns about the paper's internal processes and its capacity for self-reflection.  The author suggests that the Times' response reflects a broader, unidentified issue affecting its journalistic practices.
RECORD-00493.quote: “The news comes in code, and mostly the silences speak.” Last week, that’s how I described what happens when the New York Times reports about Judith Miller and her time in jail.
RECORD-00493.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00413.summary: This article critiques the New York Times' handling of Judith Miller's case, arguing that the paper prioritized protecting Miller over fulfilling its journalistic duty to inform the public.  Rosen contrasts the Times' perceived inaction and prioritization of its own narrative with the Washington Post's more proactive approach, highlighting a shift in his perception of the relative strengths of these newspapers.  He observes a lack of internal criticism and debate within the Times, comparing the situation to Soviet-style media control. Rosen concludes that the Times' editorial silence around Miller's actions represents a journalistic failure, questioning her understanding of journalistic ethics and the paper's subsequent defense of her.
RECORD-00413.quote: The Post, I believe, is our great national newspaper now; the Times is number two, with the Wall Street Journal close behind. Still a strong fleet.
RECORD-00413.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00364.summary: This article analyzes the Judith Miller case and its impact on the New York Times. Rosen argues that Miller's actions, while framed as a principled stand for protecting sources, ultimately damaged the newspaper's credibility and ability to report objectively. He criticizes the Times's inconsistent messaging and its failure to provide clear and comprehensive reporting on the situation, highlighting the conflict between Miller's personal decision and the institutional implications for the newspaper.
RECORD-00364.quote: There is nothing intrinsically noble about keeping your sources’ secrets. Your job, in fact, is to expose them.
RECORD-00364.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00351.summary: This article recounts a roundtable discussion between bloggers and high-level executives from mainstream media organizations. The discussion reveals a lack of innovation and entrepreneurial spirit within established media, contrasted with the agility and conversational nature of the blogosphere. While Big Media acknowledges the shift to online platforms and the growing influence of blogs, concerns remain about sustainable business models and the perceived lack of credibility in citizen journalism.
RECORD-00351.quote: “The world has really, really changed and will keep changing and we in mainstream media may not like it but its a fact and we have to embrace it or we will die.”
RECORD-00351.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00356.summary: This article analyzes the New York Times' launch of TimesSelect, a premium content package putting opinion columns behind a paywall. The author questions the Times' strategy, arguing that the exclusivity diminishes the value of opinion pieces, particularly for columnists whose influence depends on wide readership. He contrasts this with the success of bloggers who leverage the free web to reach a broader audience and offer a more timely and engaging form of commentary. The core argument challenges the Times' assumptions about the value proposition of exclusive online access to opinion pieces versus the importance of ubiquity and the power of real-time, flood-the-zone reporting.
RECORD-00356.quote: The Times Company’s press release does not seem to realize that “exclusive” opinions are not more valuable than “widely-circulated” ones— and it’s possible they will count for less.
concepts: Audience atomization overcome
Parity Product
The People Formerly Known as the Audience
RECORD-00356.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00179.summary: This open letter from Jay Rosen to the staff of CBS News reflects on the network's handling of the National Guard memos controversy a year prior. Rosen argues that the network's failure to recognize the emerging online criticism, largely from bloggers, demonstrated a disconnect from the evolving media landscape. He praises the launch of CBS News' Public Eye blog as a step towards greater transparency and engagement with online discourse, but critiques the network's continued reliance on opaque reasoning and a lack of self-awareness regarding its relationship with the internet.
RECORD-00179.quote: Transparency will absolutely change you, and it already has. If you don’t change with it, you will lose.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience
Audience atomization overcome
False balance
Mindcasting
RECORD-00179.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00352.summary: Following Hurricane Katrina, the American media's coverage shifted from deferential to aggressively critical of the Bush administration's response. This article analyzes various perspectives on this change, examining whether it represents a genuine resurgence of journalistic integrity, a simple shift in power dynamics due to the government's ineffectiveness, or a pre-existing bias manifesting more openly. The author argues that the shift in power is best understood as a triangular relationship between the press, the administration, and the public, with the government's failings creating an imbalance that empowered the media.
RECORD-00352.quote: The press gained back some of its missing authority because in this situation public authority was missing.
RECORD-00352.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00175.summary: This open thread on PressThink follows a previous post by Austin Bay arguing for a revitalized relationship between the Bush White House and the press. Rosen addresses criticism for closing comments on the previous post and encourages readers to focus on increasing their representation within mainstream media and developing better journalists, rather than dwelling on perceived media bias. He questions the underlying assumption that an objective press is unattainable and proposes a discussion about the necessary role of the institutional press.
RECORD-00175.quote: The bias discourse, however justified you may find it, is making many of you dumber by the day.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience
RECORD-00175.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00401.summary: This article is a response to Jay Rosen's piece on the Bush administration's 'rollback' strategy towards the press.  Austin Bay argues that Rosen's framing is too simplistic, ignoring the complexities of the global information war against Al Qaeda. He contends that the changing media landscape, driven by technology, has rendered the traditional 'national press' (a NY-DC-LA axis) less powerful, and that the administration's strategy should be viewed in this broader context.  Bay also points to potential biases within the traditional media, stemming from the geographic and political concentration of its editors.
RECORD-00401.quote: The press conflict and US domestic political clashes cannot be isolated from this multi-dimensional war and its harsh historical circumstances.
concepts: View from Nowhere
Rollback
The People Formerly Known as the Audience
RECORD-00401.author: Austin Bay

RECORD-00347.summary: This article reflects on a panel discussion at the AEJMC convention titled "Things I used to teach that I no longer believe." Panelists, including journalism professors and experienced journalists, shared their disillusionment with the changing landscape of journalism. The decline of a shared sense of mission, the trivialization of news in the 24-hour cycle, and the growing disconnect between journalism educators and students were discussed. The author questions the traditional ideals of objectivity and 'making a difference,' arguing that the 'official religion' of journalism has run out of gas and that a new understanding is needed for the profession's future.
RECORD-00347.quote: To learn, when you are ready to pass the torch, that some of the best and the brightest don’t want your torch, because they think it went out a while ago, counts as a sad day for J-schoolers of a certain generation.
RECORD-00347.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00534.summary: Robert Novak's on-air meltdown on CNN's "Inside Politics" is analyzed.  The incident stemmed from Novak's conflicting stances on discussing the Valerie Plame case: initially claiming he couldn't comment due to legal advice, then publishing a column disputing the CIA's account.  His subsequent refusal to answer questions about the case on CNN, culminating in a walk-off, exposed a contradiction in his public behavior and highlighted the breakdown of professional journalistic standards and the complexities of journalistic ethics when dealing with legal constraints and public accountability.
RECORD-00534.quote: Novak was about to be faced with a gigantic contradiction in his public stance, and the Network wanted it.
RECORD-00534.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00370.summary: This article presents observations from the BlogHer '05 conference, focusing on the conversations and concerns among women bloggers. The author notes the prevalent discussions surrounding the anxieties and fears associated with online identity, public discourse, and personal attacks, contrasting this with the often-overlooked anxieties experienced by journalists. The piece highlights the unique challenges and opportunities presented by the burgeoning world of women bloggers and their engagement with the public conversation.
RECORD-00370.quote: If blogging is a practice of freedom, it is completely inadequate unless it is a whole practice and to be that it must have women.
concepts: Audience atomization overcome
The People Formerly Known as the Audience
RECORD-00370.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00173.summary: This article is a preview of Jay Rosen's attendance at the BlogHer conference in 2005. He discusses the conference's goals to increase the visibility and networking of women bloggers, notes the notable attendees and speakers, and reflects on the notable absences of prominent conservative women bloggers, prompting discussion about the conference's inclusivity and the nature of online public discourse.
RECORD-00173.quote: I firmly believe that the point of weblogging is not merely to have your own blog, but to participate more fully in the public conversation. This means reading and commenting on other peoples blogs ideally at least as much as you post in your own.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience
Audience atomization overcome
Mindcasting
RECORD-00173.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00318.summary: This article discusses a Carnegie-Knight Initiative, a collaboration between five leading journalism schools and two foundations to revitalize journalism education. Orville Schell, Dean of the UC Berkeley Graduate School of Journalism, details the initiative's three main elements: research and policy, curriculum reform emphasizing interdisciplinary collaboration, and multimedia reporting laboratories. Schell addresses criticisms that the initiative is an elitist 'priesthood,' emphasizing its inclusivity and the urgent need for journalism schools to adapt to the changing media landscape and declining professional standards.
RECORD-00318.quote: What I mean by this is that the chain on which information is vectored to the public and then digested by society and the powers-that-be is broken.
RECORD-00318.author: Orville Schell

RECORD-00317.summary: This article analyzes the Bush White House's strategic rollback of the press, arguing that their approach, spearheaded by Karl Rove and others, aimed to diminish the press's influence and control the narrative. This involved non-communication, deliberate misinformation, and leveraging cultural divides to discredit journalists. The author contrasts this strategy with the previous, more collaborative model of press relations, highlighting how the Bush administration's actions challenged traditional journalistic norms and the role of the press within a democratic system. The author notes the strategy's success until the intervention of Patrick Fitzgerald's investigation, which exposed the White House's actions and brought about the moment described in the opening.
RECORD-00317.quote: The brutalizing of McClellan was no recovery of courage by a suddenly-awakened press. It was the Bush team’s bald assertiveness coming into conflict with truth collection in the criminal justice system, which has exposed a seamy story that journalists themselves would have kept hidden because it involves their confidential sources.
RECORD-00317.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00560.summary: This article discusses the controversy surrounding Robert Novak's revelation of Valerie Plame's identity as a CIA operative.  The author criticizes Novak for his actions, arguing that he facilitated an act of retribution against a whistleblower, Joseph Wilson.  Rosen calls for a professional consequence for Novak, suggesting a media-wide shunning until he explains his actions, contrasting this with Judith Miller's imprisonment for refusing to reveal her sources.  The piece explores the ethical implications for journalists involved in the case and the larger questions of journalistic ethics, source protection, and the potential chilling effect on whistleblowers.
RECORD-00560.quote: Tell me: how can journalists say with a straight face that they are concerned for future whistle blowers if one of their own, Robert Novak, together with sources made possible an act of retribution against an actual whistle blower?
concepts: He said/she said journalism
The Production of Innocence
RECORD-00560.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00304.summary: This article analyzes news coverage of Sandra Day O'Connor's retirement, focusing on the framing of the ensuing political battle as an epic showdown. Rosen critiques the journalistic tendency to present this conflict as a neutral, objective event, highlighting the inherent disconnect between the massive mobilization of activist groups and the actual impact on the Supreme Court nomination process. He argues that this framing serves the “production of innocence,” a journalistic practice that prioritizes appearing neutral over substantive analysis, ultimately obscuring the power dynamics at play and failing to explain how the media campaign is supposed to influence the outcome. The author contrasts the large-scale media operations of major news outlets with the smaller-scale, more transparent trust system of his own weblog, PressThink.
RECORD-00304.quote: All the time and money spent on campaigns may have little influence on the outcome, said several senators, because they and their colleagues see a Supreme Court vote as a deeply personal and principled decision.
concepts: He said/she said journalism
The Production of Innocence
RECORD-00304.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00553.summary: This article reflects on Norman Mailer's late-career foray into blogging, juxtaposing his unique journalistic style with the emerging landscape of online writing.  Rosen analyzes Mailer's perspective on journalism, arguing that his approach—characterized by immersive reporting and evocative prose—offers a valuable alternative to conventional news practices. The piece uses Mailer's work as a lens to explore the potential and pitfalls of online journalism, emphasizing the importance of linking, narrative depth, and engaging with the complexities of political events.
RECORD-00553.quote: The thing about journalists is that they learn about a lot of people in a hurry. Less good is that the experience is very rarely existential.
concepts: Parity Product
The People Formerly Known as the Audience
RECORD-00553.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00571.summary: This article analyzes how the Downing Street Memo story, initially ignored by mainstream media, gained traction through online blogs and activist networks, eventually forcing a reassessment of the initial news judgment.  Rosen argues that the traditional press's authority over what constitutes news is waning, replaced by a 'Court of Appeal' where online discussions and political actors can challenge and overturn initial media decisions. This shift highlights the limitations of traditional news judgment, especially in the face of powerful actors who can shape the narrative and control the flow of information.
RECORD-00571.quote: If the press ruled against you, you just weren’t news.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience
View from Nowhere
RECORD-00571.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00535.summary: This blog post reflects on the PressThink blog winning the Reporters Without Borders Freedom Blog Award.  Rosen uses this as a springboard to discuss the evolving relationship between professional journalists, bloggers, and the concept of a 'press without borders.' He argues for a universal principle of press freedom that transcends national boundaries, recognizing bloggers as legitimate participants in disseminating information and holding power accountable.  The post touches on the blurring lines between traditional journalism and citizen journalism, the challenges faced by journalists worldwide, and the potential for collaboration and shared identity across these groups.
RECORD-00535.quote: Freedom of the press belongs to those who own one, and blogging means practically anyone can own one.
concepts: Audience atomization overcome
The People Formerly Known as the Audience
RECORD-00535.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00004.summary: Jay Rosen analyzes a discussion between CNN's Bob Franken and a National Review Online blogger regarding patriotism and journalism, sparked by a passage in Alan Feuer's book. Rosen uses this exchange to explore the "newsroom religion" and its limitations, particularly regarding skepticism and national identity, questioning Franken's "citizen of the world" stance and the superficiality of the press's self-understanding as "the skeptics."
RECORD-00004.quote: How can you be a patriot and a journalist? They’re mutually exclusive occupations.
concepts: View from Nowhere
RECORD-00004.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00008.summary: This PressThink article analyzes a discussion between CNN's Bob Franken and a National Review blogger concerning patriotism, skepticism, and the role of a journalist. It explores Franken's statement that a journalist should be a 'citizen of the world' and questions the implications of this philosophy, particularly in the context of American reporters embedded with the U.S. military. Rosen uses the exchange to probe deeper into the 'newsroom religion' and the often unconscious biases that shape journalistic practice, including the concept of the journalist as 'the skeptic'.
RECORD-00008.quote: “How can you be a patriot and a journalist?” Franken had asked. “They’re mutually exclusive occupations.”
concepts: View from Nowhere
RECORD-00008.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00516.summary: This article connects the revelation of W. Mark Felt as Deep Throat with a $6 million initiative to revitalize journalism education.  Rosen argues that journalism operates under a flawed internal 'religion,' perpetuating myths like the Watergate narrative which overemphasizes the role of Woodward and Bernstein while neglecting other factors like the Senate hearings and government agencies. He critiques the ingrained beliefs and practices within journalism education, suggesting that a re-evaluation of its core tenets is necessary.
RECORD-00516.quote: Watergate, by forcing a president to resign, was an exploding supernova in the sky of journalism, blotting out the record of investigative work during Vietnam.
concepts: Newsroom Religion
The Production of Innocence
RECORD-00516.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00433.summary: This article analyzes the reaction to Newsweek's controversial article about the Quran and the subsequent media criticism.  It explores the hypocrisy of outrage directed at Newsweek's reporting while ignoring similar practices in other publications, highlighting the use of anonymous sources to create puff pieces and the lack of accountability for this behavior. The author questions the lack of a defined professional code of conduct within journalism that would allow for a stronger defense against attacks and explores various perspectives on how journalism should respond to criticism and political pressures.
RECORD-00433.quote: The real crime is not bias or secret sources. It’s fluff. It’s pseudo-sophistication. It’s a lost sense of what good journalism is all about. The real problem with investigative reporting is that it so rarely happens. The solvent for ethics in journalism is entertainment.
concepts: He said/she said journalism
The People Formerly Known as the Audience
View from Nowhere
RECORD-00433.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00575.summary: This article analyzes the Newsweek Koran story retraction, focusing on the underlying issues of trust in journalism.  Rosen argues that the incident highlights the declining public trust in the press, exacerbated by politicized attacks and outdated journalistic practices. He criticizes the 'Trust-Me Journalism' approach and advocates for improved reliability measures and updated investigative reporting standards to restore credibility.
RECORD-00575.quote: My point is journalists tend to believe the starting point is given by events themselves (rather than “decided” by them in their conventions) because their professional ideology says there are objective reasons for most everything they do. Even though they know such a thing is impossible, and incorrect as a description of how reporting and news judgment normally work.
concepts: He said/she said journalism
Verification in reverse
The Production of Innocence
Trust-Me Journalism
RECORD-00575.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00569.summary: This article analyzes Newsweek's retracted story about the alleged abuse of the Quran at Guantanamo Bay.  Rosen critiques the magazine's reliance on weak, anonymous sources and its prioritization of being first over accuracy and thorough verification. He argues that Newsweek's flawed reporting exemplifies a broader problem in journalism: insufficient standards for reliability in a world where the consequences of misinformation are amplified by instant global communication.  The article highlights the need for increased transparency and stricter sourcing standards within the profession.
RECORD-00569.quote: Under these conditions, it is imperative that journalists in the United States raise their standards for reliability, because the consequences of being wrong—for themselves, for their profession as a whole, and for others far removed—are graver.
concepts: He said/she said journalism
Verification in reverse
RECORD-00569.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00532.summary: This article analyzes the impact of Daniel Okrent's tenure as the New York Times's public editor.  Okrent's influence is seen in four key areas: changing reader representation, establishing an effective public editor's office, actively engaging with critics, and acknowledging the Times's liberal leanings.  His success stemmed from defining his role as a 'reader with access,' directly addressing reader concerns, and holding the Times accountable.  While praised for improving reader engagement and responsiveness, Okrent's approach faced criticism for perceived bias and inadequate handling of certain complaints.
RECORD-00532.quote: He changed the way readers were represented at the Times; this is to my mind his most important and far-reaching accomplishment.
concepts: Verification in reverse
The People Formerly Known as the Audience
RECORD-00532.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00221.summary: This interview with Steve Smith, editor of The Spokesman-Review, discusses the ethical implications of using a forensic computer expert posing as a 17-year-old to investigate Mayor Jim West's online activities. Smith defends the methods used, arguing that they were necessary to obtain irrefutable evidence of the mayor's actions, which ultimately led to criminal prosecution. The interview also touches upon the public's and journalists' reactions to the investigation, the resources expended, and the future of investigative journalism in a changing media landscape.
RECORD-00221.quote: But all of our ethics codes, SPJ for example, and even the Poynter’s ethics specialists, allow for exceptions when there is no other way to get the info and the story is important enough.
concepts: False balance
Verification in reverse
RECORD-00221.author: Leonard Witt

RECORD-00251.summary: This article responds to Tim Rutten's opinion piece arguing against the demise of print media. The author challenges Rutten's dismissal of civic journalism, arguing that its principles are still relevant and evolving in the context of new media technologies. The author points to the continued success and growth of online spaces dedicated to civic engagement, highlighting the work of several key figures in the field. The piece also criticizes the lack of self-reflection within newsrooms and the resulting ‘censorship by omission’ that marginalizes certain communities.
RECORD-00251.quote: What Rutten fails to realize is that much of the criticism and constructive ideas that grew out of public or civic journalism are still very much alive today, albeit with a slightly more evolved DNA.
concepts: Audience Engagement
Public Journalism
We Media
Audience atomization overcome
Civic Journalism
The People Formerly Known as the Audience
RECORD-00251.author: Leonard Witt (guest blogger)

RECORD-00190.summary: Jay Rosen's lecture explores the relationship between nation-states and their respective free presses. He argues that a free press isn't a natural phenomenon but a constructed entity, created and sustained by each nation's laws, institutions, and public rituals. He uses the historical example of the American founding to show how the press was integral to establishing a large republic, facilitating communication across vast territories. Rosen then connects this historical context to the contemporary digital revolution, predicting a time of rupture and reformation for the press as it adapts to the internet and the shift from a one-to-many to a many-to-many communication model. He anticipates questions about the definition of 'journalist' and the role of the press in a changing world.
RECORD-00190.quote: One remarkable fact in the terrible history of famine is no substantial famine has ever occurred in a country with a democratic form government and a relatively free press.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience
The Production of Innocence
RECORD-00190.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00431.summary: This article critiques the passive approach of Washington D.C. bureau chiefs in addressing the White House's use of background-only briefings.  Rosen argues that instead of politely requesting change, journalists should unilaterally stop attending these briefings, effectively ending the practice. He contrasts this direct action with the bureau chiefs' strategy of incremental pressure and criticizes media outlets for framing the situation as a negotiation rather than a choice journalists could make independently.
RECORD-00431.quote: The problem is everybody fears missing a big story and thus is afraid to say no when they know a rival will say yes.
concepts: He said/she said journalism
The People Formerly Known as the Audience
The Production of Innocence
RECORD-00431.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00208.summary: This PressThink post from May 2, 2005, discusses the declining circulation of newspapers, the rise of online news platforms like Backfence.com, and the ensuing advertising crisis. The article highlights circulation fraud lawsuits against newspapers, such as the Milwaukee Journal Sentinel, and explores the potential consequences for the industry.
