RECORD-00209.quote: Public life goes well when elections are about the issues most on the mind of the electorate, when the voters voice helps frame the choices and the debate, and the candidates are required to respond to that voice.
concepts: False balance
The Citizens Agenda
RECORD-00209.author: Chris Satullo

RECORD-00217.summary: This article analyzes the unexpected public dissemination of a private email written by Wall Street Journal reporter Farnaz Fassihi detailing her experiences in Baghdad. The email, initially intended for friends, became a widely circulated online document, sparking a debate about the boundaries between a journalist's private opinions and their public reporting. Rosen discusses the implications of this incident for the relationship between journalists, their sources, and the public, particularly in the context of the war in Iraq and the growing power of the internet.
RECORD-00217.quote: The unvarnished e-mail is not just a better read than so much conventional copy — it gives people a behind-the-curtains feeling that they love.
concepts: He said/she said journalism
View from Nowhere
The People Formerly Known as the Audience
The Production of Innocence
RECORD-00217.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00169.summary: This article analyzes the reaction of mainstream journalists to the rise of blogs, particularly in the context of the Dan Rather/CBS memo controversy. Mainstream journalists, exemplified by Nick Coleman and Tom Brokaw, viewed the bloggers' criticism as an attack on the media, failing to recognize the potential benefits of this new form of citizen journalism. Chris Satullo's article in the Philadelphia Inquirer is highlighted as a counterpoint, arguing that journalists should embrace the increased public engagement and scrutiny provided by bloggers, while also cautioning against the manipulation of the 'bias' narrative by those with ulterior motives. Satullo distinguishes between legitimate criticism seeking improvements in journalism and those seeking to destroy it through propaganda.
RECORD-00169.quote: What matters is that journalism survive, that the craft of speaking truth to power with factual care not be snuffed out.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience
View from Nowhere
RECORD-00169.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00541.summary: This article analyzes Nick Coleman's op-ed criticizing bloggers, highlighting its rhetorical style and the author's seeming satisfaction in provoking a negative reaction.  Rosen contrasts Coleman's dismissive view of bloggers with the emerging recognition of blogs' significance within journalism, citing NPR's ombudsman Jeffrey Dvorkin.  The piece underscores the changing media landscape and the mainstream media's struggle to adapt to the rise of online voices and the changing understanding of journalistic credibility.
RECORD-00541.quote: “Bloggers are hobby hacks, the Internet version of the sad loners who used to listen to police radios in their bachelor apartments and think they were involved in the world.”
concepts: Church of the Savvy
The People Formerly Known as the Audience
RECORD-00541.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00176.summary: This article presents a post-mortem analysis of Jim Lehrer's moderation of a 2004 presidential debate between George W. Bush and John Kerry. It compiles reader comments and critiques of Lehrer's performance, focusing on his question selection, perceived biases (or lack thereof), and overall effectiveness in facilitating a substantive exchange between the candidates. The discussion touches upon the role of a debate moderator in shaping public understanding of the candidates and the issues, with some arguing that Lehrer successfully steered the debate towards key policy matters while others criticized his question choices and style.
RECORD-00176.quote: His skill turned what promised to be nothing but a presentation of spin and sound bites into something more nearly debate like. In this he did citizens a great favor.
concepts: Horse-race journalism
Not the odds but the stakes
The People Formerly Known as the Audience
RECORD-00176.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00379.summary: This article discusses Adam Nagourney's decision to forgo the post-debate spin room at the 2004 presidential debate, choosing instead to write his story from Washington D.C. based solely on what the candidates said.  Rosen praises this as an act of dissent against the pervasive influence of spin in political journalism, highlighting its potential to encourage other journalists to prioritize substance over manufactured narratives. The article also explores the role of bloggers in fact-checking and holding both the press and candidates accountable.
RECORD-00379.quote: “What’s important to me is what the candidates say. I don’t care about anyone else,” he told the Miami Herald.
concepts: The Production of Innocence
He said/she said journalism
The People Formerly Known as the Audience
RECORD-00379.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00362.summary: This article critiques the 'Every Four Years Journalism' approach to election coverage, arguing that the standard model of campaign reporting—focused on horse-race dynamics, candidate profiles, and issue positions—is outdated and fails to address the changing media landscape. The author points to the rise of partisan sources like Fox News, the increased influence of blogs, and the growing public distrust of traditional media as reasons for a need for innovation in election coverage. He contrasts the complacent attitude of many established journalists, exemplified by Rick Berke of the New York Times, with the more critical and engaging approach of commentators like Jon Stewart, who are better able to connect with audiences in the age of media fragmentation and spin.
RECORD-00362.quote: Jon Stewart, who is in every sense a professional, is part of this plurality. He delivers a take on the news that is more truthful than the news for a good hunk of the audience. And so Stewart is cited by Campaign Desk for some of the most original work of the year. Often, he’s more believable than both the candidates or the press.
concepts: He said/she said journalism
View from Nowhere
RECORD-00362.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00415.summary: This article analyzes the political and journalistic fallout from the CBS 60 Minutes II report on President Bush's National Guard service.  The author critiques CBS's response to the controversy, particularly the composition and charge of its internal review committee, arguing that the network's attempts to separate itself from politics undermined its credibility and hampered a thorough investigation. The article highlights the tension between journalistic objectivity and the inherent political nature of the situation, emphasizing the need for transparent and comprehensive inquiry to restore public trust.
RECORD-00415.quote: The challenge for professional journalists today is to understand how their role has changed.
RECORD-00415.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00432.summary: Philip Gourevitch's experience covering the 2004 presidential campaign is analyzed as a case study of the limitations and complicity within the embedded press corps.  Gourevitch highlights the self-imposed constraints of the travelling press, their fear of losing access, and their complicity in accepting the candidates' controlled narratives. He argues that the press's focus on the 'horse race' and 'electability' overshadows substantive policy discussions and contributes to a 'pretend' debate. The article emphasizes the need for a more adversarial and independent press capable of challenging power.
RECORD-00432.quote: Freedom doesn’t lie in access. It means having an adversarial press, an independent press, a political press that can challenge power.
concepts: He said/she said journalism
The Production of Innocence
Pack journalism
RECORD-00432.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00467.summary: This article analyzes CBS News's handling of the controversy surrounding Dan Rather's report on President Bush's National Guard service.  The author criticizes CBS's initially hostile response to online criticism questioning the authenticity of the documents used in the report, highlighting a failure of leadership and verification processes.  The author contrasts CBS's reaction with the more self-correcting practices of other news organizations, lamenting the network's loss of credibility and the wider implications for the relationship between legacy media and the public in the age of the internet.
RECORD-00467.quote: CBS News, having now admitted that documents it relied on were inauthentic, will have troubles graver than a retraction of Dan Rather’s account and an official apology to President Bush, to CBS viewers and to the American public.
concepts: Audience atomization overcome
The People Formerly Known as the Audience
Verification in reverse
RECORD-00467.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00451.summary: This article analyzes the Dan Rather/CBS News controversy surrounding a 60 Minutes report on President Bush's National Guard service.  The report used unauthenticated documents, leading to accusations of political sabotage and a media firestorm. The author critiques Rather's response, arguing that his focus on defending his reputation and his rejection of outside investigation exacerbated the crisis.  The article highlights the clash between Rather's self-image as an incorruptible journalist and the public perception of his actions, contrasting the traditional journalistic standards with the rapid, often less rigorous judgments of the emerging blogosphere.
RECORD-00451.quote: The authenticity of the memos came under doubt almost right away. And as Miller shows, almost right away Rather began behaving under a weirdly opposite premise: That there was no doubt the memos were authentic.
RECORD-00451.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00382.summary: This article critiques the state of campaign journalism in 2004, arguing that the press has become ineffective and sidelined by political actors.  The author challenges the traditional notion of the press as neutral umpires, urging journalists to define "winning" in terms of public service and to shift their focus from politicians to citizens. The piece highlights the decline of investigative journalism due to cost-cutting measures and the rise of partisan media, resulting in a media landscape where the press is increasingly reliant on and manipulated by political interests.
RECORD-00382.quote: The press knows it can lose in the campaign struggle, and wind up reporting the news but distracting the nation.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience
View from Nowhere
RECORD-00382.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00510.summary: This article critiques the state of the mainstream media's coverage of the 2004 presidential election, focusing on the “Gang of 500”—a group of influential journalists, editors, and pundits.  Rosen argues that the media's focus on manufactured 'campaign issues' and superficial controversies like the Vietnam War overshadowed crucial policy debates and real-world problems.  He highlights the media's susceptibility to manipulation by political campaigns and the rise of cable news's emphasis on immediate, less-vetted content, ultimately leading to a loss of credibility and a diminished ability to hold power accountable. The article contrasts this 'legacy media' with the perspectives of younger voices who see news as more of a 'parity product' and are critical of the media's outdated practices and biases.
RECORD-00510.quote: The new outlets aren’t displacing the old ones; they’re transforming them. Slowly but noticeably, the old media are becoming faster, more transparent, more interactive not because they want to be, but because they have to be.
concepts: Production of Innocence
He said/she said journalism
The People Formerly Known as the Audience
RECORD-00510.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00477.summary: This article analyzes the controversy surrounding CBS News' report on President Bush's National Guard service, focusing on the allegations of forged documents.  It explores the political and cultural implications of the scandal, highlighting the role of blogs in questioning the report's authenticity and challenging the traditional media's authority. The author observes a shift in power dynamics, with blogs acting as a powerful force in investigating and disseminating information, contrasting with the slower and less analytical approach of mainstream media.
RECORD-00477.quote: The traditional news model is collapsing. It suffers from two defects. The “news object” can no longer be given sealed attributes in newspaper backrooms. The days when the press was the news object foundry are dying. Second, the news industry is suffering from its lack of analytic cells, which are standard equipment in intellgence shops.
concepts: He said/she said journalism
The People Formerly Known as the Audience
Verification in reverse
RECORD-00477.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00213.summary: This article analyzes the Miami Herald's executive editor Tom Fiedler's memo prohibiting staff from attending a Vote for Change concert, deeming it a conflict of interest. Rosen critiques Fiedler's restrictive approach, highlighting the hypocrisy of this rule compared to the Herald's own political advocacy in petitioning the Justice Department. The article explores the broader issue of press self-censorship driven by a perceived need to appease a hostile audience and the resulting pressure on journalists to sacrifice their personal lives and civic engagement for the sake of perceived objectivity.
RECORD-00213.quote: If a food writer at the Miami Herald, being also a music fan, drives to Orlando with friends to attend a Springsteen concert on the Vote for Change tour this fall, there’s an immediate problem with journalists being too partisan, but when an executive editor and political columnist signs a public petition and lobbies the Justice Department for a change in policy, that’s immediately okay, and others in the Herald newsroom can join right in.
concepts: The Production of Innocence
RECORD-00213.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00327.summary: The article discusses the declining viewership of the Republican and Democratic National Conventions and predicts a potential shift towards a single network broadcasting exclusive live coverage of the events in 2008, similar to the Academy Awards or Olympics. The author analyzes the factors driving this potential change, including declining news value, network scheduling decisions, and the increasingly partisan nature of the conventions. While acknowledging potential downsides such as limited access for those without cable, the author suggests the shift might be driven by higher ratings and streamlined promotion for both parties and networks.
RECORD-00327.quote: The Republican and Democratic parties negotiate deals with a single network to carry exclusive live coverage of the event— as with the Academy Awards, or the Olympics.
RECORD-00327.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00196.summary: This article analyzes the impact of the Swift Boat Veterans for Truth's campaign against John Kerry during the 2004 presidential election. Rosen argues that the traditional media was stunned and largely ineffective in countering the campaign's misinformation, which spread rapidly through talk radio, right-wing blogs, and Fox News. He highlights the emergence of a conservative online ecosystem that bypassed traditional gatekeepers and effectively shaped public perception, demonstrating a shift in the media landscape and challenging the established authority of the mainstream press.
RECORD-00196.quote: The reigning champion, the Mainstream Media, has been forced against all odds to accept the challenge of an upstart over the coverage of the Swiftvets controversy.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience
False balance
RECORD-00196.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00226.summary: This article describes CNN's shift in its approach to covering the 2004 Republican National Convention (RNC), moving away from the traditional isolated skybox to a more immersive, on-the-floor presence. This change aimed to bring viewers closer to the action and better capture the atmosphere of the convention. However, this new approach also presented challenges in news judgment, as the network faced the decision of whether to prioritize the convention proceedings or potentially significant events occurring outside the venue, leading to internal debate about balancing coverage and avoiding accusations of bias.
RECORD-00226.quote: “Our goal was to take our viewers into the convention hall so they experience the excitement of the convention,” he said. “To do it, we had to get out of the skybox.”
concepts: View from Nowhere
False balance
He said/she said journalism
Not the odds but the stakes
RECORD-00226.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00247.summary: This article analyzes the staging of the 2004 Republican National Convention in Madison Square Garden, contrasting it with the Democratic convention. The author observes the Republicans' deliberate creation of a smaller, more intimate stage for President Bush, symbolizing a shift towards a simpler, more controlled communication strategy. The article contrasts this with the larger, more visually cluttered stage used at the Democratic convention, and also discusses the pre-convention march as a significant event impacting the political conversation. The author reflects on the changing dynamics of political communication and the rise of alternative methods of disseminating messages beyond traditional demonstrations.
RECORD-00247.quote: Raising the floor had another advantage. It allowed for installation of a thick, and remarkably soft, bright red carpet— I mean red state red, the same red as this site and that one. Thus the floor of the arena seems luxurious and new, even a bit bouncy.
concepts: Church of the Savvy
Horse-race journalism
RECORD-00247.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00003.summary: Ahead of the 2004 Republican National Convention in New York City, major news organizations grappled with concerns about potential protests and their role in covering them.  Fear of inciting violence or unintentionally escalating situations led to security measures like unmarked news vehicles and a cautious approach to filming protests.  The article highlights the tension between journalistic responsibility to cover events and the potential for media coverage to influence or even cause unrest, drawing parallels to the 1968 Chicago protests.
RECORD-00003.quote: “The fear is that the presence of that causes it,” said David Bohrman, the executive producer of CNNs convention coverage.
concepts: The Production of Innocence
RECORD-00003.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00007.summary: The article discusses the anxieties of TV news organizations covering protests during the Republican National Convention in New York. Networks fear inciting disruptive behavior by showing up with cameras and losing control of the convention telecast. Security measures, such as concrete fortifications around Fox News headquarters, reflect the heightened tensions and concerns about potential violence and political expression.
RECORD-00007.quote: You don’t want to galvanize a crowd by pointing a camera at them. You want to report on them, but you don’t want to be the cause of them.
concepts: The Production of Innocence
RECORD-00007.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00253.summary: This article analyzes the evolving stagecraft of political conventions, specifically focusing on the 2004 Republican National Convention. It highlights the shift from traditional, formal podium presentations to more intimate, engaging formats, exemplified by President Bush's decision to deliver his acceptance speech from a small circular stage amidst delegates. The article also notes similar strategies employed by CNN and MSNBC, who moved their convention coverage to more accessible locations— a diner and a public park respectively— to foster greater audience engagement.
RECORD-00253.quote: The art and design of political conventions are advancing before our eyes.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience
RECORD-00253.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00365.summary: This article uses the physical layout of the Democratic National Convention at the Fleet Center as a metaphor for the relationship between political power, media coverage, and the audience. Rosen describes a vertical hierarchy, with the podium and television cameras at the top, effectively dictating the narrative to a distant and largely passive audience on the convention floor. He contrasts this with a past where the audience (delegates) were more directly involved in the political process, and speculates on the potential of the internet to disrupt this established power dynamic. The article also includes a section reflecting on criticism of Rosen's work, specifically comparing himself unfavorably to A.J. Liebling in a critique by Jack Shafer.
RECORD-00365.quote: When television came along, it took the action up one level, and the people on the floor became a studio audience. The people at home were the nation, looking in on what the Democrats were up to.
concepts: Audience atomization overcome
The People Formerly Known as the Audience
RECORD-00365.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00407.summary: This blog post announces the launch of Jay Rosen's 'Sky Box' blog, a project covering the 2004 Republican National Convention.  Rosen uses the metaphor of the television network sky boxes at political conventions to illustrate the changing media landscape.  He observes the shift in power dynamics from the traditional network television dominance to a more distributed media environment with the rise of online blogging and alternative platforms for disseminating information about the convention.  The post highlights the increasing importance of new media platforms in shaping the public's understanding of political events, contrasting the traditional 'sky box' perspective with the emerging opportunities for direct engagement and alternative viewpoints offered by blogs.
RECORD-00407.quote: In 2004, the view from the Network boxes doesn’t have the significance it once did.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience
View from Nowhere
RECORD-00407.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00514.summary: This article reflects on the Swift Boat Veterans for Truth campaign against John Kerry during the 2004 presidential election.  The author expresses sadness about the campaign and highlights the journalistic approach of William B. Rood, a Chicago Tribune editor, who provided a firsthand account of a Vietnam War event involving Kerry, while strictly limiting his commentary to avoid contributing to the political frenzy.  Rosen contrasts Rood's disciplined journalism with the more partisan and often misleading nature of much of the political commentary surrounding the event, lamenting the perpetuation of old conflicts and the lack of accountability from key figures like Douglas Brinkley.
RECORD-00514.quote: If the conventions of mainstream journalism prevent our media from letting readers, viewers, and listeners examine the full truth in its broadest context, then it’s time to reexamine those conventions.
RECORD-00514.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00442.summary: This article explores the impact of 9/11 on American journalism, focusing on whether the event fundamentally altered journalists' perspectives and practices.  Through an email exchange with Michael Powell of the Washington Post and reflections from other sources, Rosen examines the persistent journalistic conceit of objectivity and the challenges of admitting personal biases and worldviews. The discussion considers whether abandoning the 'no worldview' approach would improve or harm journalism, weighing the potential for greater honesty against the possible loss of rigorous reporting.
RECORD-00442.quote: Only in the fall of 2001, sitting in that library with a smoke plume spiraling up from the hole that was Ground Zero, did that long-ago plot take coherent and frightening form in my mind’s eye.
concepts: View from Nowhere
The Production of Innocence
RECORD-00442.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00414.summary: This article reflects on the impact of 9/11 on American journalism, arguing that the press failed to fundamentally re-evaluate its role and methods in the wake of the attacks.  Rosen critiques the prevailing journalistic approach, which prioritized maintaining an established 'intellectual contract' with readers over a deeper reckoning with the changed context of war and terrorism. He highlights the limitations of a purely journalistic framework for understanding such a world-altering event and questions whether the traditional ethics and methods of journalism remained adequate in the 'war on terror'.  The piece also touches on the role of media in disseminating information about terrorism, considering the ethical implications of sharing graphic content.
RECORD-00414.quote: Terrorism works best in an open society, where news flows. Those who keep the flow going, and react to emergencies by making news of them, sustain terror by doing their job.
RECORD-00414.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00460.summary: Juan Gonzalez reflects on the 2004 UNITY convention, arguing that the lack of diversity in newsrooms stems from systemic issues within journalism education and the industry itself. He criticizes the haphazard and misdirected efforts of media executives to integrate newsrooms and advocates for a more inclusive approach involving minority journalists in creating solutions.  He proposes a joint convention of major journalism organizations in 2008 to foster dialogue and improve diversity in the profession.
RECORD-00460.quote: Any program aimed at eliminating the vestiges of racial and ethnic exclusion in American newsrooms will have a greater chance of success if it includes from its inception the ideas and thoughts of those who have been historically excluded.
RECORD-00460.author: Juan Gonzalez

RECORD-00279.summary: Terry Heaton, a former TV news director, reflects on the challenges of achieving editorial diversity in newsrooms. He argues that simply hiring minority reporters is insufficient; the issue lies in how these reporters are integrated and utilized within the newsroom. Heaton observes resistance from some minority reporters to cover stories related to their own communities, stemming from fears of tokenism and type-casting. He also notes that career advancement concerns often overshadow commitment to journalistic ideals among minority journalists.
RECORD-00279.quote: Diversity means recognizing the talents of the individual because of who they are, not because of what they are: Black. So, you can send me to Washington to cover the big story understanding that I’ll bring a different set of eyes, a different confluence of experiences, a different insight, to the story than someone white would. It may, or may not, be a better story, but it will be a different story, a diverse story, a yet untold story.
concepts: False balance
RECORD-00279.author: Terry Heaton

RECORD-00393.summary: This article is a response to criticism of the UNITY: Journalists of Color convention, where attendees applauded Senator John Kerry more enthusiastically than President Bush.  Sotomayor defends the convention, arguing that the criticism is misplaced, as the lack of diversity in the media predates the event and that the convention served a crucial purpose in raising important issues often overlooked in mainstream media. He contends that UNITY's advocacy for diverse and representative journalism is not inherently liberal and compares their actions to those who fought for press freedoms in the past.
RECORD-00393.quote: We advocate for fair, representative, accurate journalism, by changing the complexion of newsrooms, not just racially and ethnically, but through the natural diversity of thought that occurs when you bring in people with different backgrounds.
RECORD-00393.author: Ernest Sotomayor

RECORD-00234.summary: This article presents a debate on the ethics of journalists publicly expressing their political opinions, particularly in the context of the 2004 Unity: Journalists of Color convention. Letters from various journalists and commentators discuss whether showing partisan preference (e.g., applauding a candidate) undermines journalistic credibility and professionalism. The central question revolves around balancing a journalist's role as a citizen with their professional responsibilities, and whether transparency about personal political leanings is necessary or harmful to their work.
RECORD-00234.quote: I think it’s been that extreme philosophy of detachment from the real world that has made our journalism so irrelevant to most “regular” people and branded us as disconnected, clueless elites.
concepts: View from Nowhere
False balance
RECORD-00234.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00194.summary: The 2004 Unity: Journalists of Color convention, the largest gathering of journalists ever in the U.S., sparked a debate about the intersection of journalists' political views and professional ethics. A standing ovation for John Kerry by many attendees raised concerns about journalistic impartiality, particularly from critics who argued the display showed partisan bias. The author examines the differing perspectives on this incident, including those who defend the journalists' right to political expression outside of work and those who emphasize the importance of maintaining a perceived neutrality in the public eye. The article also touches on the broader issue of diversity within journalism and the challenges of achieving genuine representation.
RECORD-00194.quote: Journalists risk losing their credibility if they let their politics show, said Bob Steele, an ethics specialist at the Poynter Institute, a school for journalists in St. Petersburg, Fla. They should be “observers guided by the principle of independence,” he said.
concepts: View from Nowhere
False balance
Horse-race journalism
RECORD-00194.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00363.summary: This article discusses the challenges and opportunities of event blogging, focusing on the 2004 Democratic National Convention. It emphasizes the importance of understanding the audience and their needs, framing the blog as a four-way transaction between the event, the blogger, the users, and the broader blogosphere. The author highlights the failure to obtain crucial information (like the convention's music playlist) as an example of the disconnect between the event and the bloggers trying to cover it, demonstrating a lack of transparency and access that hindered effective reporting.
RECORD-00363.quote: The solution to “what is the right framework for event blogging?” begins with a prior problem: finding, attracting and “holding” in one place—hopefully, at your blog—a motivated and interested-in-this-event user base.
RECORD-00363.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00228.summary: This 2004 Editor & Publisher column by Jay Rosen examines the prevalent self-identification of journalists as "moderates" in response to accusations of liberal bias in newsrooms. Rosen argues that this self-reported moderation, rather than indicating ideological centrism, might represent a belief in the irrelevance of personal political views in journalistic practice. He contrasts this "Newsroom Joe" approach with an alternative perspective advocating for transparency regarding journalists' political affiliations to enhance accountability and credibility. The piece highlights the debate between these two approaches and calls for a more nuanced understanding of journalistic objectivity.
RECORD-00228.quote: When 54% of national journalists and 61% of local journalists decline the labels “liberal” and “conservative” and identify instead as moderates, according to the Pew Center, what are they really saying?
concepts: View from Nowhere
False balance
RECORD-00228.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00244.summary: This article details Jay Rosen's experience covering the 2004 Democratic National Convention as a blogger, reflecting on the challenges and opportunities of using a blog as a reporting platform. He invites readers to participate in a public debriefing, encouraging interaction and feedback on his approach to covering the convention and the broader implications of blogging for political journalism.
RECORD-00244.quote: The blogging of Boston goes on because the campaign does.
concepts: Audience atomization overcome
The People Formerly Known as the Audience
RECORD-00244.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00294.summary: This article is a debriefing of the 2004 Democratic National Convention, focusing on the evolving relationship between mainstream media and blogs. The author observes a significant shift in how journalists perceive blogs, noting increased adoption and attention from mainstream outlets. He predicts a future where blogging will become commonplace, losing its novelty, but the interactive platform of blogging as a tool for public conversation will remain important. The discussion touches upon the ritualistic aspects of political conventions, and the lack of coverage of these ritual elements by mainstream media. The author questions whether the significance of 'blogging' itself will fade, while the underlying practice of self-publishing and online public discourse will persist.
RECORD-00294.quote: I believe the period when we talked this way—blogs, bloggers, blogging—will be ending sooner rather than later, and those who feel it their business to track down and slay with satire “blog triumphalism” will have to find other work.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience
Audience atomization overcome
RECORD-00294.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00505.summary: This blog post reflects on the author's experience covering the 2004 Democratic National Convention in Boston, focusing on the overwhelming security presence and the contrasting coverage by bloggers and traditional media.  The author argues that the intense security, a response to the threat of Al Qaeda, represented a significant, underreported story reflecting the changed national and global condition. He contrasts this with bloggers' focus on less consequential matters, and discusses the emerging relationship between bloggers and traditional journalists, highlighting both the potential and limitations of each.
RECORD-00505.quote: The security situation, which dominated the event (but the event had to suppress it) was trying to tell us a story, which it is the job of politics and political leaders to articulate.
RECORD-00505.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00342.summary: This article offers observations on the 2004 Democratic National Convention, focusing on the prevalent 'message-speak' used by pundits, the disproportionate focus on swing voters, the use of music in network broadcasts, and the creation of a 'split public' in televised election analysis. The author critiques the reductive nature of political commentary that prioritizes tactical messaging over genuine communication and engagement with the audience, highlighting how television tries to position viewers as informed insiders while portraying the rest as passive masses.
RECORD-00342.quote: Message speak is reductive— therefore easy.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience
Verification in reverse
RECORD-00342.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00492.summary: This blog post discusses the author's interaction with a journalism professor, Thomas McPhail, who is critical of bloggers' lack of commitment to journalistic ethics.  The post then features an interview with Washington Post reporter Thomas Edsall, who offers a more positive perspective on the role of blogs in journalism, highlighting their ability to challenge journalistic groupthink and uncover overlooked stories, such as the Trent Lott controversy. The author concludes by mentioning an agreement to blog the Republican National Convention for Knight-Ridder.
RECORD-00492.quote: The blogs can sort of break the ice and make it clear that there is something pretty strange or pretty unique or pretty interesting or pretty awful about something that, given our way of looking at things— which tends to be very straight line: is it illegal, is it this, will somebody criticize it?
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience
View from Nowhere
RECORD-00492.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00512.summary: This article reflects on the 2004 Democratic National Convention, analyzing how the event's organizers strategically adapt to the fragmented media landscape.  The author interviews Rod O'Connor, the convention's CEO, who explains the approach of delivering the Democratic 'message' across multiple platforms (television, blogs, talk radio) to reach a dispersed audience.  Rosen contrasts this 'message delivery' approach with other, more impactful forms of political communication, such as a poignant anti-war protest using empty boots, highlighting the limitations of viewing political conventions primarily as a 'television show' designed to deliver information.
RECORD-00512.quote: On Thursday night when John Kerry stands up there and gives his speech, you know that’s our Super Bowl, that’s it, that’s what this whole thing is about. And it’s my job to make sure we get to that point, the air is clear and everything’s focused on him that night.
concepts: Audience atomization overcome
The People Formerly Known as the Audience
RECORD-00512.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00263.summary: This article reflects on the 2004 Democratic National Convention, analyzing the absurdity of the event as a televised spectacle and its significance as a ritualistic memory device for the political parties and the press. The author questions the press's continued investment in the convention, arguing that its news value has diminished, and contrasts this with the growing interest in bloggers as a representation of the future of political coverage. The article also includes an interview with the Convention's CEO and discusses the implications of granting press credentials to bloggers.
RECORD-00263.quote: Journalists sense this about conventions— the way they point backward.
concepts: He said/she said journalism
Horse-race journalism
False balance
RECORD-00263.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00548.summary: This article discusses the prevailing media narrative of the Democratic National Convention as a staged event, contrasting it with the perspective of bloggers who are attending.  The author highlights the irony of thousands of journalists covering an event they deem essentially meaningless, while acknowledging the potential of bloggers to offer a different, more engaged perspective rooted in citizen participation and a less cynical view of political events.
RECORD-00548.quote: What do the bloggers bring to this? My short answer to the press is: everything you have removed.
RECORD-00548.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00360.summary: This article discusses the unprecedented inclusion of bloggers in covering the 2004 Democratic National Convention. The author reflects on the excitement and skepticism surrounding this development, highlighting the contrasting viewpoints of established journalists and bloggers themselves. Concerns about inflated expectations, the potential for bias, and the role of bloggers as an alternative filter for news are explored, along with observations on the media's coverage of the bloggers' involvement.
RECORD-00360.quote: Political blogs have crawled from the Web’s primordial ooze, evolving into a mutant strain of journalism.
RECORD-00360.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00455.summary: The assassination of Paul Klebnikov, an investigative journalist for Forbes Russia, highlights the inherent political nature of journalism, especially in unstable political environments.  Klebnikov's work, focused on exposing corruption among Russian oligarchs, directly challenged the existing power structures and ultimately cost him his life.  The article contrasts Klebnikov's active engagement with Russian politics through his journalism with the often apolitical stance adopted by journalists in more stable democracies, questioning whether the latter approach is truly possible or even desirable.
RECORD-00455.quote: You can say of Paul, without exaggeration, that he gave his life for the truth.
RECORD-00455.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00278.summary: This article reflects on the 2004 political conventions, examining the changing role of journalism in the digital age. It discusses the increasing influence of blogs and bloggers, contrasting their approach to covering the conventions with that of traditional media. The author highlights the limitations of traditional coverage, which often focuses on pre-determined narratives and lacks depth, while praising bloggers for their ability to provide more nuanced perspectives and capture the atmosphere of the events. The piece also explores the theoretical frameworks of communication, contrasting the 'transmission' and 'ritual' views, and considers how these perspectives apply to the changing media landscape.
RECORD-00278.quote: A ritual view of communication is directed not toward the extension of mesages in space but toward the maintenance of society in time;” not the act of imparting information but the representation of shared beliefs.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience
Audience atomization overcome
RECORD-00278.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00557.summary: This article contrasts the conventional, factual reporting of the 2004 Democratic convention with Norman Mailer's evocative, stylistic coverage of the 1960 Democratic convention.  It argues for a more literary and immersive approach to political convention coverage, emphasizing the writer's ability to capture the mood and atmosphere beyond the surface-level facts and figures.
RECORD-00557.quote: For once let us try to think about a political convention without losing ourselves in housing projects of fact and issue.
RECORD-00557.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00475.summary: This article critiques Alex Jones's Los Angeles Times piece on bloggers at the Democratic National Convention. Rosen argues that Jones undervalues the contributions of bloggers, misrepresents their intentions, and exhibits a bias against the emerging online media landscape.  He highlights the symbiotic relationship between established journalism and the burgeoning blogosphere, advocating for mutual understanding and respect rather than dismissal. The piece sparks a discussion among various bloggers and commentators about the legitimacy of online journalism and the evolving media ecosystem.
RECORD-00475.quote: Political conventions have become festivals of faux harmony and candidate image-building, which makes them marvelous targets for blogging’s candor, intelligence and righteous wrath.
concepts: Church of the Savvy
The People Formerly Known as the Audience
RECORD-00475.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00245.summary: This article critiques the state of political campaign coverage in the US media, arguing that it is stale, predictable, and focused on superficial aspects like polls and media strategy rather than substantive issues. The author contrasts this with the potential for fresh insight from bloggers gaining media credentials, questioning why established journalists seem incapable of similar renewal. He suggests the problem stems from journalism's failure to understand the ritualistic nature of political campaigns and its inability to analyze the political process as a form of performance comparable to Hollywood productions.
RECORD-00245.quote: To the truly religious person, Reality is unthinkable without reference to the metaphysical dream given to him by his religion.
concepts: Church of the Savvy
Horse-race journalism
Not the odds but the stakes
RECORD-00245.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00224.summary: This interview with Steve Rubel discusses Jay Rosen's perspective on participatory journalism, its democratic potential, and its challenges. Rosen defines participatory journalism as citizens actively engaging in news creation and interpretation, often using blogs and online tools. He highlights the positive aspects of this trend, such as increased citizen engagement and the democratization of information. However, he also acknowledges the potential downsides, including the inherent problems associated with freedom of information online. The conversation touches upon the role of bloggers in extending and interpreting news coverage, comparing them to a 'second wave' that builds upon initial reporting. Rosen also speculates on the future of journalism, suggesting that journalists who effectively utilize blogs within established media outlets will be key in transforming the profession.
RECORD-00224.quote: Public relations, if it wants to do good, should stand for real transparency in organizations, and genuine interacivity with publics.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience
Audience atomization overcome
Mindcasting
RECORD-00224.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00357.summary: This article analyzes the evolution of political conventions from genuine political events with unpredictable outcomes to carefully staged media productions. The author traces this shift from a time when conventions determined nominees and featured real political debate, through the rise of television's influence and the prioritization of image and message control. The result, according to Rosen, is a loss of newsworthiness and a reliance on ironic commentary as a substitute for substantive reporting, a situation further complicated by the nascent presence of webloggers at the convention.
RECORD-00357.quote: The crisis in narration is not a problem you solve.
RECORD-00357.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00408.summary: This article critiques Dan Rather's statement that "seconds count" in journalism, arguing that the emphasis on speed often overshadows the deeper understanding and meaning of events.  Using the example of the transfer of sovereignty in Iraq, the author demonstrates how the competitive race to be first often conflicts with the need for thorough reporting and contextualization. The article highlights the limitations of focusing on speed over substance, particularly in complex political events where symbolic meaning and communication to various audiences are crucial.
RECORD-00408.quote: But for somebody like Dan Rather and Christiane Amanpour, what really matters is not exactly when you tell a waiting world that a handover happened, or who is on the air first, but your ability to say what happened, and to comprehend fully— but quickly—the nature and meaning of the event.
RECORD-00408.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00444.summary: This article is an open letter to Bill Gates offering advice on how to create a successful blog.  Rosen argues against a blog focused on Microsoft or technical details, suggesting instead a newsy blog where Gates shares his opinions on global issues, politics, and current events. He emphasizes authenticity and a personal voice, advocating against the use of ghostwriters and promoting a culture of freedom of speech within Microsoft for employee bloggers.
RECORD-00444.quote: An original weblog by Bill Gates—rich, famous, powerful, controversial person—could be a fourth way a business titan deals with the press: as author and critic, reading the headlines, putting certain ideas at risk, inserting himself into public conversation as a citizen of the planet, a reader of the news, (a sharp, funny person) editing the Web like all good weblogs do, and finding a honest voice in which to speak.
concepts: The Production of Innocence
The People Formerly Known as the Audience
RECORD-00444.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00372.summary: This article analyzes the Bush administration's relationship with the press, arguing that the administration actively disengaged from reality and from critical voices, both within its own ranks and in the media. The author suggests that the administration prioritized its own beliefs over factual evidence, leading to flawed policies and a lack of accountability. The piece also critiques the New York Times' coverage of the Iraq War, highlighting instances of journalistic failure and the need for greater transparency and self-reflection within the news organization.
RECORD-00372.quote: The biggest mistake I made on Iraq was to believe that the Bush administration would want to get Iraq right more than it wanted to prove its own prejudices right.
RECORD-00372.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00568.summary: This article analyzes the debate surrounding media bias, particularly a Pew Research Center survey showing a higher percentage of journalists identifying as liberal.  It examines the reactions from various sources, including Editor & Publisher's intention to further investigate the issue, and critiques the framing of the debate as a 'bias war,' arguing that it often obscures the underlying issue of attack politics and the blurring lines between journalism and propaganda, particularly exemplified by Fox News.
RECORD-00568.quote: In a war zone thinking has to become automatic; that’s one of the costs of war.
RECORD-00568.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00207.summary: This article analyzes the enduring anecdote of Lesley Stahl's interview with a Reagan White House official, Dick Darman, who famously said, "Nobody heard what you said." The author examines how this story, initially a seemingly amusing anecdote about the power of visuals over words in television news, evolved into a narrative explaining Reagan's political success and the perceived impotence of the press. Rosen critiques the story's widespread adoption as a simplistic explanation for Reagan's popularity, arguing it obscures more complex political factors and fosters a cynical view of the public's media consumption.
RECORD-00207.quote: Ronald Reagan has this wonderful communicator’s ability to convey to the public: “I know you’re smarter about some things than I am, and I know there are some things we both perhaps don’t understand as well as we’d like. I know that experts drive you crazy like they sometimes drive me crazy. Let’s see if we can get right to the heart of this issue. We’re talking about freedom, the American way, evil empires, patriotism, some of the old eternal values that seem to have been shunted aside.”
concepts: The Production of Innocence
False balance
RECORD-00207.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00487.summary: This article analyzes two contrasting news articles—one from the New York Times and another from the Washington Post—covering the same subject: misleading political advertisements in the 2004 election.  The author highlights the difference in their conclusions: the NYT piece presented a 'both sides do it' narrative, while the Washington Post article explicitly stated that the Bush campaign engaged in more distortion.  Rosen argues that the Post's approach, while potentially perceived as biased, is necessary for the mainstream press to regain its credibility as a truth-teller in an era of declining influence and increased online information fragmentation. He advocates for a shift away from the 'he said, she said' model to a 'he said, she said, we said' approach, where news organizations actively assess and declare their conclusions about truthfulness, leveraging independent fact-checking resources to support their assertions.
RECORD-00487.quote: “The traditional sources of news in America are losing influence and have not yet recognized it,” wrote Vaughn Ververs of the National Journal, just today.
concepts: He said/she said journalism
Verification in reverse
RECORD-00487.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00214.summary: This PressThink post celebrates reaching 250,000 recorded visits since its inception in September 2003. Rosen expresses gratitude to readers and highlights various popular and impactful posts, categorized by themes like most linked, most criticized, most commented on, and most consequential, offering a retrospective on the blog's content and impact.
RECORD-00214.quote: If you didn’t exist, I wouldn’t be doing this.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience
Horse-race journalism
RECORD-00214.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00410.summary: This article analyzes the New York Times' evolving approach to transparency, using the Wen Ho Lee case (2000) and the Iraq War weapons of mass destruction coverage (2004) as case studies.  The author argues that sustained criticism from peers and the impact of Jayson Blair scandal pushed the Times toward greater self-assessment and public acknowledgment of errors, spurred in part by increased online scrutiny and the changing dynamics of media power in the digital age.
RECORD-00410.quote: The New York Times had no descriptive term for what it published because what it published described deeds that have always gone nameless in the paper’s imaginary, although these actions are quite evident to others.
RECORD-00410.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00423.summary: This article analyzes the intense debate surrounding media coverage of the Iraq War, particularly focusing on the criticisms levied against the press for its portrayal of the Abu Ghraib prison scandal and the overall conflict.  The author examines accusations of bias, explores the defense strategies employed by journalists and news organizations, and ultimately argues for a more transparent and openly political approach to justifying news decisions, recognizing that such decisions often involve weighing competing political considerations rather than solely adhering to an objective 'reality principle'.
RECORD-00423.quote: The news from Iraq is not too negative; it’s too narrow.
RECORD-00423.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00306.summary: This Q&A addresses the pervasive nature of bias in journalism, arguing against the unattainable goal of unbiased reporting. Rosen contends that human judgment inherently shapes journalistic work, and the pursuit of objectivity through the removal of various influences (political parties, publishers, etc.) ultimately leads to a flawed ideal. He suggests that prioritizing good judgment over the elimination of bias is a more realistic and desirable approach to journalistic practice.
RECORD-00306.quote: Journalism is saturated with judgment, and a lot of that judgment belongs to the individual journalist.
concepts: He said/she said journalism
The Production of Innocence
View from Nowhere
RECORD-00306.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00530.summary: This article analyzes the challenges faced by journalists reporting from Iraq in the wake of the US-led invasion.  The author discusses the increasing dangers faced by correspondents, leading to self-imposed restrictions on movement and a reliance on embedded reporting with the US military.  The article uses the experiences of John Burns, a New York Times reporter, as a case study to illustrate the ethical and practical dilemmas involved in reporting from a war zone, highlighting the risks faced by journalists and the potential for overlooking human rights abuses. The author also questions the role of journalists in such situations and their responsibility towards both their safety and the accurate representation of events.
RECORD-00530.quote: If they’re not going out in Baghdad, but sticking to quarters, then reporters cannot really cover what they are there to cover— the ongoing war, the re-building of Iraq, the emergence of a new Iraqi state and its politics, and the changing situation on the ground.
RECORD-00530.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00412.summary: This article discusses the contrasting responses of mainstream media and online blogs to the Nick Berg beheading video.  Mainstream media outlets largely chose not to publish graphic images or video, citing concerns about taste and sensitivity.  However, bloggers widely shared the content, arguing that the public's right to know and the importance of confronting the reality of terrorism outweighed these concerns. This event sparked a debate about news judgment, the role of the internet as an alternative news source, and the political implications of media decisions.
RECORD-00412.quote: “The people have news judgment,” Jarvis wrote (May 14.) “And it beats the judgment of many an editor.”
concepts: He said/she said journalism
The People Formerly Known as the Audience
View from Nowhere
RECORD-00412.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00328.summary: Tom Bettag's Fred Friendly First Amendment Award speech critiques the failings of network news in the lead-up to 9/11, arguing that prioritizing business over viewers' trust jeopardizes the integrity of journalism. Bettag advocates for a realist approach, acknowledging the commercial nature of network news but emphasizing the crucial role of maintaining public trust to ensure the long-term success and relevance of the industry. He recounts the history of network news's struggle against corporate pressures and emphasizes the need for news organizations to prioritize viewers over advertisers.
RECORD-00328.quote: News on network television is a business— period. Get every other starting point out of your head, he advises. If you begin another way, like “news is a public trust” or “separation of church and state,” you will only confuse things, and delude yourself. “You work for a television company, an entertainment company run by people who may, or may not, give a damn about news.”
RECORD-00328.author: Jay Rosen

RECORD-00216.summary: This article analyzes the political statements made surrounding Ted Koppel's Nightline broadcast of the names of fallen soldiers in Iraq. The author argues that various entities, from Sinclair Broadcasting's refusal to air the segment to individual bloggers' commentary, engaged in political discourse, highlighting the inherent politicization of seemingly neutral acts. The article further examines Koppel's justifications for his broadcast, contrasting them with interpretations that frame the broadcast as inherently political, and discussing the challenges of maintaining the perception of 'political innocence' in journalism.
RECORD-00216.quote: I am opposed to sustaining the illusion that war can be waged by the sacrifice of the few without burdening the rest of us in any way. I oppose the notion that to be at war is to forfeit the right to question, criticize, or debate our leaders’ policies.
concepts: View from Nowhere
False balance

The author explores the Bush administration's 'Bush Thesis,' which posits that the press is a self-interested 'special pleader' with declining influence, and examines the implications of this perspective on the relationship between the presidency and the media.

RECORD-00215.summary: This article discusses the controversy surrounding Karen Ryan, a public relations professional who narrated a video news release (VNR) posing as a reporter. Following criticism, the Public Relations Society of America (PRSA) released a statement acknowledging the misleading nature of this practice, although stopping short of a ban. The author analyzes the PRSA's response, contrasting it with the swift action taken by journalistic organizations, and explores the broader implications of the increasing normalization of fakery in both journalism and public relations.
RECORD-00215.quote: The significance of these statements is not that they transform a dubious practice. RECORD-00509.summary: This article reflects on a discussion surrounding the relationship between blogging and journalism, sparked by a BloggerCon session led by the author.  The central question is whether blogging constitutes journalism, and the author finds that a rigid definition is unhelpful.  Instead, he proposes a more nuanced understanding, recognizing the distinct yet overlapping characteristics of both forms, and suggesting that a productive future involves integrating the conversational nature of blogging with the reliability of established journalism.
RECORD-00509.quote: Blogging is not journalism. When we separate these two things, we honor both.

RECORD-00486.summary: This article analyzes President George W. Bush's decision to hold a prime-time press conference, questioning the strategic logic behind choosing this format over a direct address to the nation.  The author explores the conflicting narratives surrounding the event – the White House's justification of addressing public concerns and regaining control of the political narrative versus the underlying contempt for the press as a perceived 'special interest group'. The author argues that the effectiveness of the press conference hinges on the press being viewed as a legitimate critic, a condition undermined by the administration's own rhetoric.  The article concludes by reflecting on the handling of questions about mistakes, highlighting the inherent tension between the administration's desire for infallibility and the public's right to accountability.
RECORD-00486.quote: The news conference will give Bush a forum to address concerns that have caused a dip in his election-year popularity.

RECORD-00480.summary: This article analyzes the fallout from a controversial comment made by blogger Markos Moulitsas Zuniga (Daily Kos) regarding the deaths of American mercenaries in Iraq.  The Kerry campaign's subsequent removal of a link to Kos's blog highlights the evolving relationship between political campaigns and online bloggers.  The author explores the tension between the 'weak' and 'strong' theories of linking, arguing that the Kerry campaign's decision reveals a lack of understanding of the online world and the potential for uncontrolled negative publicity arising from associated content.  The incident underscores the challenges of navigating the nascent political landscape of the early internet and raises questions about the role of blogs in political campaigns.
RECORD-00480.quote: If you are going to be in politics, you have to play by the political rules.

Ryan's presentation mimicked a news report, sparking controversy and criticism. The author uses this case to explore the Bush administration's calculated contempt for the press, its attempts to control the news agenda, and the blurring lines between PR, journalism, and political propaganda.  The article highlights the erosion of press power and the willingness of PR professionals to employ deceptive tactics to influence public opinion, ultimately questioning the role of journalistic ethics and the public's ability to discern truth from manufactured news.

RECORD-00167.summary: This article, a preparatory essay for a BloggerCon discussion, argues that journalism is a practice, not a profession, and that it's independent of its delivery method. While professional journalists set a high standard, the accessibility of weblogs expands the possibility of citizen journalism, increasing democratic participation in information dissemination. The author emphasizes the importance of considering what journalism is good for and why it matters, rather than focusing on the binary question of whether weblogs are 'journalism'.
RECORD-00167.quote: Journalism is a demanding practice; and only in principle—a pretty important principle—is “anyone” or “everyone” able to do it.

RECORD-00230.summary: This eulogy for Neil Postman reflects on his teaching style, which involved challenging students' existing beliefs to foster genuine learning. Rosen highlights Postman's focus on human communication, his mistrust of technology, and his unique ability to identify individual learning needs. The piece uses anecdotes from Rosen's personal experiences as a student of Postman to illustrate his pedagogical approach and emphasizes the social nature of memory and learning.
RECORD-00230.quote: There aren’t any teachers until there are learners, and there aren’t any learners until something is disturbed in the student’s world.

RECORD-00281.summary: This article is a critique of "strategy coverage" in campaign journalism. Rosen argues that this type of reporting, which focuses on the candidates' strategic calculations and media manipulation, serves no clear public purpose and is a bankrupt form of journalism. He criticizes the lack of transparency and the inherent bias towards the 'inside' perspective, ultimately advocating for a shift towards more substantive political reporting.
RECORD-00281.quote: Kathleen Hall Jamieson (bio) says that strategy coverage is identified by five features: 1.) winning and losing are the central plot device, 2.) metaphors of war, competitive sports and game theory are prevalent in the account, 3.) politics is assessed as theatre, with performers, critics and audiences, 4.) performance, style, appearance, and “perceptions” of the candidate are commonly examined, 5.) opinion polls and the candidate’s standing in them are a baseline reality.

The Times had criticized Scalia for speaking at an advocacy group's event but had not reported on Ginsburg's similar involvement. Patterico's blog alerted the Times to this omission, leading to a subsequent article correcting the imbalance. This event highlighted the potential for a 'two-way relationship' between bloggers and established media, demonstrating the power of citizen journalism and online media watchdogs in holding traditional media accountable.

It highlights the role of bloggers in pushing the story into the national conversation, acting as a corrective to the herd mentality and lack of historical context within established newsrooms. The author argues that bloggers, though not originating much original reporting, served as a crucial filter, providing necessary historical background and fostering a counter-conversation that ultimately led to Lott's resignation.  The 24-hour news cycle is criticized for its inherent limitations in fully assessing the significance of events.
RECORD-00502.quote: News stories, says Josh Marshall in the report, have a 24 hour audition on the news stage, and if they dont catch fire in that 24 hours, theres no second chance.

The author questions the press's tendency to default to established narratives instead of engaging in more imaginative and critical reporting.  Using Jonathan Schell's book *History in Sherman Park* as an example, the author advocates for a shift in journalistic perspective, suggesting that reporters should focus more on the reception of political messages by ordinary citizens rather than simply relaying campaign narratives.  The piece further proposes alternative framing of election coverage, such as considering the Democratic primaries as a two-front war between the Dean forces and the party establishment, urging reporters to rotate their images of politics to create more insightful and accurate reporting.

RECORD-00441.summary: This article critiques the traditional job description of a journalist during campaign season, arguing that it is outdated and fails to account for the expanded roles journalists have assumed.  The author points to journalists' involvement in 'screening the field' of candidates, shaping narratives, driving news frenzies, and influencing political outcomes, all tasks beyond the traditional observer role.  The article calls for a new job description that acknowledges journalists' influence and responsibilities, and offers a more honest and nuanced understanding of their role in the political process.
RECORD-00441.quote: No one elected the press, yet the press is now an intimate part of everything having to do with elections. The press is not there to make political decisions, yet everything the press does helps shape those decisions. The author highlights the democratizing potential of weblogs, enabling individuals to become publishers and compete with established media, exemplified by cases like Chris Allbritton's independent war reporting and Andrew Sullivan's success in attracting readers through his blog.

Rosen highlights the inherent contradictions in the commonly held belief that journalists can be simultaneously neutral and effective critics of power, ultimately arguing for a more self-aware and politically engaged approach to journalism.

The author, drawing on Clay Shirky's analysis, argues that the campaign created a "bubble of belief" fueled by the internet's ability to lower coordination costs and foster a sense of movement, but this online fervor didn't translate into actual votes. The article further critiques the mainstream media's reliance on insider knowledge and its failure to accurately gauge public opinion, highlighting the limitations of both traditional campaign reporting and the overly optimistic assessments of the internet's impact on politics.

Nangle, a reporter for the Worcester Telegram & Gazette, expressing his frustration with the prevalent horse-race coverage in mainstream political journalism. The article uses Nangle's experience to highlight the pressures faced by reporters to conform to pack journalism and the risk of losing out professionally by deviating from established conventions.  Rosen examines the inherent conflict between journalistic competition and the homogenization of coverage, proposing that bloggers could potentially support reporters who challenge the status quo.

A significant portion focuses on Rosen's role as an ambassador for weblogs, highlighting the prevailing skepticism among established journalists about weblogs' potential to replace traditional news media. Rosen argues for a more nuanced understanding of the relationship between amateur and professional journalism, emphasizing the unique contributions of weblogs and citizen journalists.

dissertation-1986.summary: Rosen's doctoral dissertation traces the history of the idea that the function of the press is to inform the public. It argues that the rise of the mass circulation newspaper, while creating a technical ability to reach everyone, actually undermined the conditions necessary for a "universal town meeting." Drawing heavily on Walter Lippmann and John Dewey, it suggests that the professionalization of journalism ("objectivity") was a retreat from the problem of creating a genuine public life in a complex society. It contrasts news as "symptom" vs. news as "symbol" and explores how the press creates a "pseudo-environment" of public opinion.
dissertation-1986.quote: An impossible press was born, one which sought to solve the whole problem of public life simply by controlling the conduct of journalists.

RECORD-00085.summary: NYU's Studio 20: Digital First program prepares the next generation of journalists for the digital age by focusing on practical, project-based learning in collaboration with established media companies and digital startups. The program aims to equip students with skills to innovate in digital newsrooms, bridge business, editorial, tech, and audience challenges, and regain public trust.
